| Sync `retry` on both Applications | Without one a failed apply ends the operation where it fell; one flake at the front of the chain, such as the ESO webhook being unreachable on a fresh CNI, leaves every issuer and certificate behind it unmade |
| `ServiceMonitor` rendered unconditionally | The chart cannot sync until the Prometheus operator CRDs exist, which is why they are the separate `prometheus-operator-crds` Application — see [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/#crds>) |
| Two webhook replicas, a PodDisruptionBudget and a hostname spread | The webhook's `failurePolicy` is `Fail`, so while a single replica reschedules through a Kured drain every Certificate and Issuer apply is refused — see [Replica placement](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/#replica-placement>) |
| `letsencrypt-staging` and `letsencrypt-prod` | Use staging first: production allows five duplicate certificates per week, a misconfigured solver retries until that is gone, and there is no appeals process |

The IAM user needs at minimum:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["route53:GetChange", "route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets", "route53:ListHostedZonesByName"],
  "Resource": "*"
}
```

## Usage

Store the credentials once OpenBao and ESO are up; `make bao-secrets` prompts for them, or by hand:

```bash
bao kv put kv/cert-manager/route53 \
  access-key-id="YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID" \
  secret-access-key="YOUR_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"
```

ESO creates the `route53-credentials` Secret within its `refreshInterval`, or [immediately on request](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/#adding-a-secret>).

## Health check

Work down the chain of custody; the answer is nearly always further back than the `Certificate`:

```bash
kubectl describe certificate -n kube-system <name>
kubectl get certificaterequest,order,challenge -A
kubectl -n cert-manager logs deploy/cert-manager --tail=100
```

A `Challenge` stuck in `pending` is a DNS problem: either the credentials cannot write to the zone, or the TXT record is there and the resolver has not caught up. `dig +short TXT _acme-challenge.<host>` settles which.

## Pitfalls

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A sealed OpenBao means no renewals**
>
> Until OpenBao is unsealed and the secret stored, cert-manager cannot issue or renew, and the failure surfaces as an expired certificate roughly two months later — see [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#pitfalls>).

# Cilium

Cilium is the CNI, and on this cluster considerably more: it replaces `kube-proxy`, terminates ingress through Gateway API, hands out LoadBalancer addresses on a network with no cloud load balancer, encrypts node-to-node traffic, and shows what is talking to what. That consolidation is the argument for it on bare metal, and the reason a broken Cilium is never a small problem.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system` |
| Depends on | The Gateway API and Prometheus operator CRDs it renders against, and a `k8sServiceHost` that answers |
| If it is down | Everything. No CNI, no service routing, no ingress, no LoadBalancer addresses |
| Health check | `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium status --brief` |
| UI | `hubble.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` (Hubble); the same flows in 3D across namespaces at [Flowscape](<https://homelab-apps.wlkr.ch/flowscape/>) |
| Files | `payload/platform/cilium/` |

## Configuration

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `kubeProxyReplacement: true` | Service routing in eBPF. `proxy.disabled` in `ansible/templates/kubeadm.yaml.j2` keeps `kube-proxy` out at init and on every `kubeadm upgrade apply` |
| `k8sServiceHost` as a literal IP | With `kube-proxy` gone Cilium cannot reach the API server through a Service, so it names the [control-plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>) — see [Pitfalls](<#pitfalls>) |
| Gateway API | Replaces an Ingress controller — see [Gateway API](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md>) |
| `lb-pools.yaml` | One address each for the apps and infra Gateways, announced over L2 ARP so the LAN can find them |
| `bgp.yaml` | The same two addresses as `/32` routes over eBGP from every control-plane node to the router. The router forwards traffic it routes, from other VLANs, VPN clients and port forwards, to all three nodes at once and drops a dead one after the hold time, where L2 moves one lease. L2 stays because the addresses sit inside the flat LAN, whose hosts ARP for them and never ask the router. The ASNs and timers are in `bgp.yaml`. The router side is FRR on the UDM Pro: `make config` renders it from the inventory's `router_*` variables into `output/router/frr-bgp.conf`, so a firmware reset is recovered by pasting that file |
| `encryption.type: wireguard` | Transparent node-to-node encryption |
| Hubble, behind the [Authentik](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md>) proxy outpost | Hubble has no authentication of its own; the HTTPRoute points at the outpost and a ReferenceGrant in `payload/platform/authentik/` permits the cross-namespace reference |
| Hubble metrics labelled by namespace | The chart's Hubble dashboards filter on source and destination namespace and show nothing without them; namespace keeps the series count to the square of the namespace count. The HTTP metric adds workloads, but only for traffic Cilium proxies at L7, which is the Gateway. |
| `hubble.export.static` | Every flow with a `DROPPED`, `ERROR` or `AUDIT` verdict, and every HTTP request a policy proxies at L7, goes to a file on the node that [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) tails into Loki, with a field mask that keeps identities, ports and the request line and drops the rest. Hubble's own buffer is minutes deep; this is the record of what a policy refused after the fact, and of the requests the L7 rules are tightened from. Other forwarded flows are not exported: thousands a second on a cluster this size, where the proxied requests are a few. |
| `hubble.redact` | Every header except `User-Agent` and `Content-Type`, and the password of a basic-auth URL, is replaced before a flow leaves the agent, for the export file and Relay alike. An L7 rule proxies the requests that carry credentials: External Secrets' `X-Vault-Token`, the bearer tokens Prometheus scrapes with, Velero's signed S3 requests, Authentik's cookies. The method, path and query the L7 rules are tightened from survive |
| `hostFirewall.enabled: true` | Filters traffic to the node's own addresses, which is every host-networked port, with `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` objects that select nodes. Attaching it denies nothing on IPv4 until a policy selects the node; IPv6 is another matter, see [Pitfalls](<#pitfalls>). Rollout and policy in [Host firewall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/#host-firewall>) |
| `policyAuditMode: false` | Policies are enforced. On, verdicts are logged and not enforced, which is how a rollout's observation week runs — see [Security Policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/#rollout>). Cluster-wide, and blind to L7 rules |
| `rollOutCiliumPods` and the four `rollOutPods` | The agent, Envoy, the operator, Relay and the UI read their ConfigMap once, at startup. With a checksum of it on the pod template, a merged value rolls the pods and is live within minutes, and a value the agent refuses fails at merge time, while someone is watching, not at the next unrelated restart. The price is that every change to `cilium-config` is a rolling restart of the CNI on every node: running pods keep their networking, policy updates pause per node for the seconds its agent is down, and the [`k8sServiceHost` pitfall](<#pitfalls>) bites at merge, not later |
| `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable: 1` | The chart default restarts the agent on two nodes at once, which can be two of the three control planes that hold the L2 leases and BGP sessions; one at a time keeps every Gateway address announced throughout a rollout |
| `operator.replicas` above one | The operator owns Gateway API reconciliation, LoadBalancer IP allocation and the `cilium-secrets` sync; with one replica, a drain or crash of its node stalls all three until the reschedule. The chart's hostname anti-affinity keeps the replicas apart, so the standby is already running — see the [operator pitfall](<#pitfalls>) |
| `lb-pools.yaml` on `cilium.io/v2` | The storage version for `CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool`; `v2alpha1` is served as deprecated and warns on every sync. `CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy` has no `v2` yet and stays |
| `cilium-agent` memory limit | It is the one process whose death takes pod networking with it, so it was sized from a week of measurement, not a day, before the [platform rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md>) applied |
| `trustCRDsExist: true` | The chart otherwise refuses to render while `monitoring.coreos.com/v1` is missing: the bootstrap install, a render before `prometheus-operator-crds` has synced, and the diff preview's throwaway cluster |

## Usage

### Installation

Cilium is installed twice, in a sense. `make install-cilium` installs it by Helm, because no pod runs without a CNI and ArgoCD is a pod; ArgoCD then adopts the release. The version comes from `targetRevision` in `application.yaml` — see [Version pins](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md>).

The bootstrap install uses the same `values.yaml`, and has to: the pods roll whenever `cilium-config` changes, so a slimmer bootstrap config would restart every agent the moment ArgoCD adopts the release. The Gateway API CRDs go in first because the operator checks for them once, at startup. The one difference is the three `serviceMonitor.enabled` flags, which `make` turns off because the Prometheus operator CRDs arrive through ArgoCD; ArgoCD adds the monitors back on adoption, rolling the agent and operator once.

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium status --brief
```

The BGP session on each control-plane node, `established` with two routes advertised. `bgp.yaml` selects the control planes only, so ask that node's agent rather than whichever pod `ds/cilium` resolves to:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$(kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l k8s-app=cilium \
  --field-selector spec.nodeName=<control-plane> -o name)" -- cilium bgp peers
```

Hubble answers *what did I just break?* during a network policy rollout — see [Security Policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/#usage>). The `hubble` CLI talks to Relay through a port-forward on its default port:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system port-forward deploy/hubble-relay 4245:4245 &
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --follow
```

The same verdicts, for the whole Loki retention window, in Grafana:

```text
{job="hubble", verdict="DROPPED"} | json | flow_drop_reason_desc="POLICY_DENIED"
```

## Pitfalls

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **`k8sServiceHost` pointed at an address that does not answer takes the cluster down**
>
> Every Cilium pod loses the API server at once, and cluster networking goes with it — including whatever you were using to fix the problem. The change ordering is in [Control Plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **An operator that starts without the API server leaves the Gateways without certificates**
>
> cilium-operator checks for the Gateway API CRDs once at startup; if that check fails it runs without its Gateway controller until the next restart, and `cilium-secrets` empties. Envoy then resets the TLS handshake on every node without a cached copy, so some clients fail and others do not, depending on which node the router hashes them to. `CiliumGatewayCertificatesMissing` fires; `kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deploy/cilium-operator` recovers it.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **A chart default that disappears stays in `cilium-config`**
>
> The bootstrap install's `helm` field manager still co-owns every `cilium-config` key it wrote, so ArgoCD's server-side apply cannot delete one the chart stops rendering. When a chart release dropped the `envoy.xdsMode` default, the agents kept `envoy-xds-mode: ads` while Envoy's bootstrap switched to split xDS; Envoy got no listeners, and every Gateway and L7 policy stopped forwarding. Pin such a value in `values.yaml` rather than relying on the default.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **The host firewall drops all node IPv6, with or without a policy**
>
> With `enable-ipv6: false` the datapath has no IPv6 branch, so on the native device and `cilium_host` every IPv6 packet is dropped as `DROP_UNKNOWN_L3` in both directions, before any policy or audit mode ([upstream](<https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/47307>)). A node keeps its SLAAC address until the lifetime runs out, and a client that does not fall back to IPv4 stalls until then. The drops reach Loki as `DROPPED` flows with a reason other than `POLICY_DENIED`, so `HubblePolicyDrops` stays quiet.

# CloudNativePG

Every chart that needs PostgreSQL ships its own, each upgraded by whoever maintains the chart that buried it. CloudNativePG is one operator in `cnpg-system` and a `Cluster` resource per database.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `cnpg-system` for the operator; each database in its workload's namespace |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for the database volumes and the backup buckets; [cert-manager](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md>) for the backup plugin's gRPC certificates |
| If it is down | Running databases keep running; failover, upgrades and new clusters stop |
| Health check | `kubectl get clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io -A` → `Cluster in healthy state` |
| Backups | Continuous WAL and a nightly base backup per database, to a bucket of its own |
| Files | `payload/platform/cloudnative-pg/` |

## Configuration

A `Cluster` is not a StatefulSet with a nicer name:

| It handles | Instead of |
| --- | --- |
| Primary election and failover between instances | A single pod that takes the database down with it |
| `-rw` and `-ro` Services that follow the primary | Hardcoding a pod name and being wrong after a restart |
| Rolling minor-version upgrades, replicas first | A `StatefulSet` image bump and hope |
| Generated credentials in a `-app` Secret | A password in Git, or a manual `kubectl create secret` |
| A PodMonitor and an upstream Grafana dashboard | No visibility until something is already wrong |

Major-version upgrades are declarative too, but offline: ArgoCD reports Degraded while one runs and the workload is down for its duration. Read [the upstream guide](<https://cloudnative-pg.io/documentation/current/postgres_upgrades/>) before merging one.

Databases claim `rook-ceph-block`, so Ceph's three copies already sit under every database and a single-instance `Cluster` is a defensible default: the data survives a node loss even when the process does not. Where a workload cannot tolerate the restart, `instances: 3` is the change, as [Authentik](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/#database>) shows.

The operator itself runs two replicas (`replicaCount` in `application.yaml`'s `valuesObject`), spread per [Replica placement](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/#replica-placement>): the same pod serves the `Cluster` and `ScheduledBackup` admission webhooks with `failurePolicy: Fail`, so a single replica rescheduling through a Kured drain refuses every apply, while leader election keeps one of the two reconciling. The chart ships no PodDisruptionBudget.

### Backups

The [Barman Cloud plugin](<https://cloudnative-pg.io/plugin-barman-cloud/>) runs beside the operator and injects a sidecar into every instance that names an `ObjectStore`. The sidecar archives each WAL segment as PostgreSQL closes it and takes the base backups a `ScheduledBackup` asks for, so a database restores to any second inside the retention window, not just to last night.

| Choice | Why |
| --- | --- |
| The plugin, not `spec.backup.barmanObjectStore` | The in-tree field is deprecated upstream and is removed in a later release |
| One bucket per database, claimed in its own namespace | The bucket's keys exist only there, so a compromised workload can read or delete its own backups and nobody else's |
| `https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch`, not the plain RGW Service | Backups hold every row of the database; the Gateway's TLS is the same path Velero uses |
| Base backup nightly, after Velero | The two never contend for the object store; WAL archiving covers the hours between |
| `retentionPolicy` equal to `schedules.ttl` in `payload/platform/velero/application.yaml` | One window to reason about: what Velero can no longer restore, the WAL archive cannot either. Change the two together: each `backup.yaml` restates the value |
| Preview databases have none | They are rebuilt from the pull request and deleted with it |

`ObjectStore` is a namespaced resource with no cluster-scoped counterpart, so the per-database part is a short, identical stanza (below); everything else is shared: the plugin, and the `cnpg-backups` policy in `payload/platform/security/network-policies/cluster-wide.yaml` that lets any CloudNativePG pod reach the object store.

## Usage

### The contract

**Every workload that needs PostgreSQL gets a CloudNativePG `Cluster`. No chart-bundled database, ever.** A bundled Postgres moves when the application's chart decides — a major version jump inside someone else's patch release; a `Cluster` moves when its `imageName` changes, a Renovate PR with a human in front of it. Most bundled subcharts are also Bitnami's, whose registry terms keep changing. The rule for the [workloads repository](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/add-workload/index.md>):

1. Disable the subchart (`postgresql.enabled: false` or `internalDatabase.enabled: false`) and point the chart at the `Cluster`.
2. Never copy the password. CloudNativePG writes `username`, `password`, `host`, `port`, `dbname` and a ready-made `uri` to `<cluster-name>-app`; charts take those through an `existingSecret` block, and applications without one read `uri` as an environment variable. Nothing goes into Git or OpenBao — nothing outside the cluster ever needs this secret.
3. Put the `Cluster` in the workload's namespace, not `cnpg-system`, so the namespace's `CiliumNetworkPolicy` governs port 5432 and deleting the namespace takes the database with it.
4. Set `enablePDB: false`. The operator's `<cluster>-primary` PodDisruptionBudget refuses the primary's eviction outright, so a node drain hangs on it until [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) gives up and the node is never rebooted. Without the budget a single instance is down for the move to another node and a three-instance cluster fails over within a minute.
5. Back it up with the [stanza below](<#backing-up-a-database>). Velero's nightly PVC snapshot is crash-consistent and restores only to the night it was taken; the WAL archive restores to any second.

### Backing up a database

Next to the `Cluster`, in the same namespace, with `<db>` the cluster's name. The bucket name is cluster-wide, hence the namespace in it; the sync wave puts the store ahead of the `Cluster` that names it.

```yaml
---
apiVersion: objectbucket.io/v1alpha1
kind: ObjectBucketClaim
metadata:
  name: <db>-backup
  namespace: <namespace>
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-2"
spec:
  bucketName: cnpg-<namespace>
  storageClassName: ceph-bucket
---
apiVersion: barmancloud.cnpg.io/v1
kind: ObjectStore
metadata:
  name: <db>
  namespace: <namespace>
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-2"
spec:
  retentionPolicy: 14d
  configuration:
    destinationPath: s3://cnpg-<namespace>/
    endpointURL: https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch
    s3Credentials:
      accessKeyId: {name: <db>-backup, key: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}
      secretAccessKey: {name: <db>-backup, key: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}
    wal:
      compression: gzip
    data:
      compression: gzip
---
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: ScheduledBackup
metadata:
  name: <db>
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  schedule: "0 0 3 * * *"
  immediate: true
  backupOwnerReference: self
  cluster:
    name: <db>
  method: plugin
  pluginConfiguration:
    name: barman-cloud.cloudnative-pg.io
```

And in the `Cluster`:

```yaml
  plugins:
    - name: barman-cloud.cloudnative-pg.io
      enabled: true
      isWALArchiver: true
      parameters:
        barmanObjectName: <db>
```

`enabled: true` is the webhook's default; written out, ArgoCD's diff matches the live object, since `plugins` is compared as a whole list. Adding the plugin restarts every instance to inject the sidecar: a single-instance database is down for that restart, a replicated one switches over. `immediate: true` takes the first base backup at once, so the WAL archive is restorable from the first day.

## Health check

```bash
kubectl get clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io -A
kubectl cnpg status -n <namespace> <cluster-name>
```

`Cluster in healthy state` is the phrase; ArgoCD's built-in health check reads the same field, which lets a sync wave wait for a database before the application in front of it. The plugin prints the primary, replication lag, WAL position and last failover.

```bash
kubectl get backups.postgresql.cnpg.io -A           # Phase completed, one per night
kubectl get clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io -A \
  -o custom-columns='NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,ARCHIVING:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="ContinuousArchiving")].status'
kubectl get objectstores.barmancloud.cnpg.io -A -o yaml | grep -A3 serverRecoveryWindow
```

`ContinuousArchiving` `True` means the last WAL segment reached the bucket; `False` means WAL is piling up on the instance's volume, which fills it. The recovery window lives on the `ObjectStore`, per server name: the `Cluster`'s own backup fields and the `cnpg_collector_*_backup_timestamp` metrics stay empty with a plugin, which upstream documents as deprecated under CNPG-I. `prometheusrule.yaml` therefore reads the `ObjectStore` and `Backup` objects through kube-state-metrics' [custom resource metrics](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/#scrape-targets>): `CNPGBackupStale` when a server's last successful base backup is older than the rule's threshold, `CNPGBackupFailed` when a recent Backup ended in `failed`. Both are warnings on the daily mail.

## Pitfalls

- **A stuck archive fills the volume.** PostgreSQL keeps every WAL segment the sidecar has not archived; a broken bucket or policy shows as `ContinuousArchiving` `False` long before the PVC is full. Fix the cause, never delete `pg_wal`.
- **A dead replica fills the primary.** Its replication slot holds WAL until the replica catches up, so every multi-instance `Cluster` caps it with `max_slot_wal_keep_size` at a quarter of the volume; past that the slot is invalidated and the replica restores from the WAL archive or must be recreated with `kubectl cnpg destroy <cluster> <instance>`.
- **A full volume is not resized by the operator.** An instance stopped with `no free disk space for WALs` keeps its PVC size although `storage.size` grew; patch that PVC to the new size by hand, as [upstream documents](<https://cloudnative-pg.io/documentation/current/instance_manager/>) under "Disk full failure".
- **A restore is a new `Cluster`.** Recovery bootstraps a fresh cluster from the bucket; it never rewinds a running one. Give the new cluster its own `ObjectStore` destination, or its archive would mix with the one it was restored from.

## Recovery

### Point-in-time restore

1. Pick the target time (UTC) and check it lies inside the window:

```bash
kubectl -n <namespace> get objectstore <db> -o jsonpath='{.status.serverRecoveryWindow}{"\n"}'
```

1. In the workloads repository, add a second `Cluster` named `<db>-restore` beside the original, which stays untouched: every Application prunes, so a renamed `Cluster` is a deleted one. It bootstraps from the old store, keeping the old name as `serverName`:

```yaml
  bootstrap:
    recovery:
      source: origin
      recoveryTarget:
        targetTime: "2026-10-21 12:00:00+00"
  externalClusters:
    - name: origin
      plugin:
        name: barman-cloud.cloudnative-pg.io
        parameters:
          barmanObjectName: <db>
          serverName: <db>
```

Its own `plugins` entry keeps the same `barmanObjectName` with `serverName: <db>-restore`, so the new archive lands beside the old one.

1. Merge and wait for `Cluster in healthy state`; both databases now run, and the application still reads the original.
2. In a second PR, point the application at `<db>-restore-app`, set the `ScheduledBackup`'s `cluster.name` to `<db>-restore`, and delete the original `Cluster`; the sync prunes it.

# Descheduler

The scheduler places a pod once and never looks at it again. After [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) drains a node, everything that lived there restarts on the others and stays there when the node comes back, so a cluster that has rebooted through an update ends up with one idle node and the rest loaded. The [descheduler](<https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/descheduler>) runs on a schedule, evicts a few pods from the loaded nodes, and lets the scheduler place them where there is room.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `descheduler` |
| Depends on | [metrics-server](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/metrics-server/index.md>) for the node usage `LowNodeUtilization` compares |
| If it is down | Nothing visible: pods stay where the last drain left them |
| Health check | `kubectl -n descheduler get jobs` → the last run `Complete` |
| Files | `payload/platform/descheduler/application.yaml` |

## Configuration

The values are in `payload/platform/descheduler/application.yaml`; the reasoning:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `kind: CronJob` with a `schedule` | A Deployment would poll continuously for a cluster that changes shape once per Flatcar update. A pass every few hours drifts a rebooted cluster back into balance the same day |
| `nodeFit: true` | A pod is only evicted when another node has room for it, so an eviction never turns into a Pending pod |
| `podProtections.extraEnabled: PodsWithPVC` | Ceph volumes would follow an evicted pod, but the pods that own them run alone: a moved [CloudNativePG](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md>) primary is a failover and a cold restart of its application, a moved Loki a detach and reattach. Their PDBs are off so that Kured can drain, so this is the only guard. `emptyDir` pods stay protected at the default because their data goes with them |
| System-critical pods at the default | `evictSystemCriticalPods` stays off, so nothing with `priorityClassName: system-cluster-critical` is ever moved. Those components hold their own placement rule instead — see [Replica placement](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/#replica-placement>) |
| `maxNoOfPodsToEvictPerNode` and `evictionLimits.node` | A few pods per node per pass: one Kured reboot already moved everything on a node once, a second mass move is what this component is meant to avoid |
| `LowNodeUtilization` with `metricsUtilization.source: KubernetesMetrics` | Usage comes from metrics-server, not from requests. Requests here are still being tuned and many are far below what the pod uses, so a requests-based view would call a loaded node idle |
| `thresholds` and `targetThresholds` | A node under the low mark is a candidate to receive, one over the high mark a candidate to lose pods; nodes in between are left alone |
| `RemoveDuplicates` and `RemovePodsViolatingTopologySpreadConstraint` for both `DoNotSchedule` and `ScheduleAnyway` | After a drain, replicas of one workload sit on the same node; both plugins put them back on separate ones. Soft constraints count too, because the scheduler honoured them only until the drain |
| `RemovePodsHavingTooManyRestarts` | A pod in a restart loop for hours is more likely stuck on its node than broken; a move is cheap and the restart count resets |
| Metrics off | A CronJob pod exists for seconds; a `ServiceMonitor` would scrape an empty Service |

## Usage

Nothing to operate. To watch a pass:

```bash
kubectl -n descheduler create job --from=cronjob/descheduler manual-$(date +%s)
kubectl -n descheduler logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=descheduler --tail=100
```

Every eviction is an event on the pod, so `kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=Descheduled` shows what moved and why.

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n descheduler get cronjob,jobs
kubectl -n descheduler logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=descheduler --tail=100 | grep -i "evict\|error"
kubectl top nodes    # what LowNodeUtilization sees
```

## Pitfalls

- **It only evicts, never schedules.** Where a pod lands is the scheduler's decision; the descheduler assumes the scheduler will do better the second time, which holds after a drain and not much else.
- **It honours PodDisruptionBudgets.** An eviction that would violate a PDB is refused. The single-instance [CloudNativePG](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md>) clusters carry none, so that Kured can drain; `PodsWithPVC` is what keeps the descheduler off them.
- **One pod per over-utilized node per pass** when usage comes from metrics-server. A badly skewed cluster takes several passes, which is the point of running it on a schedule rather than once.
- **A move is a restart.** Anything without a second replica is briefly down when it is evicted; `nodeFit` guarantees a place to go, not zero downtime.

# external-dns

[external-dns](<https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/external-dns/>) creates the Route53 records for this cluster's hostnames from the `HTTPRoute`, `TLSRoute` and `GRPCRoute` objects that already declare them. Without it every hostname is a record made by hand in the AWS console, a step that lives nowhere in the repository and leaves a record pointing at nothing when the workload goes.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `external-dns` |
| Depends on | [External Secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md>) for its Route53 credential, [Gateway API](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md>) for the HTTPRoutes it reads |
| If it is down | New hostnames get no DNS record. Existing records are left alone |
| Health check | `kubectl -n external-dns logs deploy/external-dns --tail=50` |
| Files | `payload/platform/external-dns/` |

## Configuration

In `application.yaml`'s `valuesObject`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Sources `gateway-httproute` and `gateway-grpcroute` | Every HTTP and gRPC hostname here is a route; the address comes from the route's parent `Gateway`, so nothing is written down twice. The `GRPCRoute` is Argo CD's, see [CLI access](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/#cli-access>) |
| `target` annotation on `apps-gateway` | The cluster sits behind NAT, so the Gateway's own address is a LAN one nobody outside can reach. external-dns reads the public address off the Gateway, not the routes, so every `*.k8s.wlkr.ch` record gets it once. `infra-gateway` has none: those names stay LAN-only on purpose |
| Source `gateway-tlsroute` | The agents' SSH hostnames are `TLSRoute`s, one per session. This version reads `TLSRoute` `v1`, the version installed, so each session's record appears with its route and no wildcard record exists to maintain; see [SSH listener](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/#ssh-listener>) |
| Domain filter | Nothing outside that subtree is touched |
| TXT registry with an owner id | A companion `_externaldns.*` TXT record stamps every record it creates, and it only modifies or deletes records carrying that stamp. Hand-made records in the same zone are invisible to it |
| Policy `sync` | Deleting an HTTPRoute removes its record. Safe only because of the registry; without it `sync` would happily delete your MX records |
| `--aws-zone-match-parent` | The records live in the `wlkr.ch` zone, not a zone of their own |
| A second entry in `domainFilters` | `wollbi.ch` is a zone of its own in the same account, for the neighbourhood sites. Without it their routes are ignored rather than refused, which reads as external-dns being down |
| `ssh.wlkr.ch` in `domainFilters` | Same zone as `k8s.wlkr.ch`, a different subtree |
| Credentials as a file (`AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE`), not environment variables | The environment puts a key that can repoint every hostname into `kubectl describe pod`, crash dumps and every child process. The `ExternalSecret` templates an INI `credentials` key, the only key mounted; the original keys stay in the Secret so nothing still reading them breaks |

The credential is a separate IAM user and OpenBao path from cert-manager's — see [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#kv-layout>) for why. Its policy needs `route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets` on the hosted zone, plus `route53:ListHostedZones` and `route53:ListResourceRecordSets`.

## Usage

Nothing beyond the `HTTPRoute` you were already writing — see [Gateway API](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/#usage>). The credential is stored once, by `make bao-secrets` or by hand:

```bash
bao kv put kv/external-dns/route53 \
  access-key-id="AKIA..." \
  secret-access-key="..."
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n external-dns logs deploy/external-dns --tail=50
dig +short argo.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch
kubectl -n external-dns port-forward deploy/external-dns 7979:7979
curl -s localhost:7979/metrics | grep endpoints_total
# external_dns_source_endpoints_total   8   <- hostnames it can see
# external_dns_registry_endpoints_total 0   <- records it owns
```

`All records are already up to date, there are no changes for the matching hosted zones` means it found no zone to change: sources fine, provider not, which on Route53 is usually zone matching.

## Pitfalls

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A record that will not update is one external-dns does not own**
>
> Check for the matching `_externaldns.` TXT record in Route53. To adopt a hand-made record, create that TXT entry or delete the record and let external-dns recreate it.

# External Secrets Operator

[External Secrets Operator (ESO)](<https://external-secrets.io/>) bridges [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) to native Kubernetes `Secret` objects. Workloads consume secrets the standard way — `envFrom`, `volumeMounts`, `imagePullSecrets` — with no sidecar, no init container and no code that knows what a Vault token is.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `external-secrets` |
| Depends on | [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) at runtime, though not to be installed |
| If it is down | Secrets already materialised keep working. Nothing rotates, and nothing new resolves |
| Health check | `kubectl get clustersecretstore` → `Valid` on all three |
| Files | `payload/platform/external-secrets/`; the stores in `payload/platform/openbao/cluster-secret-store.yaml` |

## Configuration

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Workload
    participant ES as ExternalSecret
    participant ESO as ESO Controller
    participant Bao as OpenBao
    participant K as K8s Secret

    ESO->>Bao: login (k8s SA JWT)
    Bao-->>ESO: vault token
    ESO->>Bao: read kv/path
    Bao-->>ESO: secret data
    ESO->>K: create/update Secret
    App->>K: mount / envFrom
```

ESO mints a short-lived token for an `external-secrets-vault` ServiceAccount through the TokenRequest API, which the chart's controller ClusterRole allows in every namespace (`cluster-secret-store.yaml` binds its own `external-secrets-vault-token-creator` ClusterRole, scoped to that ServiceAccount name, beside it); OpenBao validates it against the TokenReview API and issues a token bound to that store's policy. Platform namespaces use the `openbao` store and the ServiceAccount in `external-secrets`; a workload uses `openbao-apps` and its own, which confines it to `kv/<namespace>/` — see [Kubernetes auth](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#kubernetes-auth>). No long-lived credential exists anywhere. The stores use ESO's `vault` provider unchanged against the in-cluster Service.

In `application.yaml`'s `valuesObject`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| No `ClusterSecretStore` here | A store only validates against a running, unsealed OpenBao, so it ships with `openbao`, whose readiness it reports — see [Bootstrap convergence](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/#bootstrap-convergence>) |
| Webhook ServiceAccount token stays mounted | The webhook has no RoleBinding but builds an in-cluster client at startup and exits without the token (`unable to load in-cluster config`), which only shows when the pod is recreated |
| Two webhook replicas, a PodDisruptionBudget and a hostname spread | The webhook's `failurePolicy` is `Fail`, so while a single replica reschedules through a Kured drain every `ExternalSecret`, `PushSecret` and store apply fails and the Argo sync that carried it goes to retry — see [Replica placement](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/#replica-placement>) |

## Usage

### Adding a secret

1. Store the value in OpenBao, following the [KV layout](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#kv-layout>). A random value is not typed in at all: a `Password` generator and a `PushSecret` write it, see [Generated secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#generated-secrets>).

   ```bash
   bao kv put kv/<workload>/<purpose> key1="value1" key2="value2"
   ```
2. Declare an `ExternalSecret` alongside the workload's other manifests; the parent Application picks it up. A workload names `openbao-apps` and ships the ServiceAccount that store logs in as; a platform component names `openbao` instead and needs no ServiceAccount:

   ```yaml
   ---
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: ServiceAccount
   metadata:
     name: external-secrets-vault
     namespace: my-app
     annotations:
       argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-2"
   automountServiceAccountToken: false
   ---
   apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
   kind: ExternalSecret
   metadata:
     name: my-app-credentials
     namespace: my-app
     annotations:
       # ESO's CRDs arrive with the external-secrets Application; this
       # covers a sync before they have landed.
       argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true
   spec:
     refreshInterval: 1h
     secretStoreRef:
       name: openbao-apps
       kind: ClusterSecretStore
     target:
       name: my-app-credentials   # name of the resulting K8s Secret
       creationPolicy: Owner
     data:
       - secretKey: key1           # key in the K8s Secret
         remoteRef:
           key: my-app/<purpose>   # the namespace is the prefix
           property: key1          # key inside the KV entry
   ```

   To pull every key without listing them, use `dataFrom` instead of `data`:

   ```yaml
   spec:
     dataFrom:
       - extract:
           key: <workload>/<purpose>
   ```
3. Consume the Secret:

   ```yaml
   spec:
     containers:
       - name: my-app
         envFrom:
           - secretRef:
               name: my-app-credentials
   ```

`refreshInterval` polls OpenBao; `0` disables polling and re-syncs only on resource changes. To sync now rather than wait:

```bash
kubectl annotate externalsecret -n <namespace> <name> \
  force-sync=$(date +%s) --overwrite
```

## Health check

Start with the store; if it is not Ready, nothing downstream is either. `openbao-apps` and `openbao-claude-agents` report `Valid` without logging in, so their auth failures show on the `ExternalSecret` instead:

```bash
kubectl get clustersecretstore openbao -o jsonpath='{.status}' | jq
```

| Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| OpenBao is sealed | [Unseal it](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#unsealing-after-a-restart>) |
| Kubernetes auth role missing | `make bao-policies` writes all three roles; it needs a [root token](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#generating-a-root-token>) |
| Wrong `serviceAccountRef` | `external-secrets-vault`, in `external-secrets` for `openbao` and without a namespace for the other two |

Then the individual object:

```bash
kubectl describe externalsecret -n <namespace> <name>
```

| Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| The KV path does not exist (`bao kv get kv/<path>` returns 404) | Store the secret first |
| `property:` matches no key in the KV entry | `bao kv get kv/<path>` lists them |
| `permission denied` from `openbao-apps` | The path is outside `kv/<namespace>/`, or the namespace has no `external-secrets-vault` ServiceAccount |
| `using cluster store ... is not allowed from namespace` | The store's `conditions` exclude the namespace: a workload on `openbao`, or a platform namespace on `openbao-apps` |

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Rotation does not restart anything**
>
> A rotated value reaches the `Secret` within `refreshInterval`, but a pod that read it into an environment variable keeps the old one until something restarts it. A rollout, or Reloader-style tooling, is the other half of rotation.

# Gateway API

The [Kubernetes Gateway API](<https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/>) replaces the Ingress resource, implemented by Cilium for both load balancing and TLS termination. The improvement is the split in ownership: the cluster owns the `Gateway` — addresses, certificates, ports — and each app owns its own `HTTPRoute`.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system`, where Cilium runs |
| Depends on | [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md>) to implement it, [cert-manager](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md>) for the wildcard certificates |
| If it is down | Nothing reaches any hostname. Running pods keep running |
| Health check | `kubectl -n kube-system get gateway` → both `PROGRAMMED=True` with an address |
| Files | `payload/platform/gateway-api/`, `payload/platform/gateway-api-crds/` |

## Configuration

Two Gateways in `kube-system`, each with a dedicated address from the Cilium L2 pool, defined in `gateways.yaml`. `apps-gateway` serves user-facing workloads under the router's public address; `infra-gateway` serves the platform UIs, LAN only. A route names a listener by `sectionName`:

| Gateway | Listener | Hostnames | Certificate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `apps-gateway` | `https` | `*.k8s.wlkr.ch` | `apps-gateway-tls` |
| `apps-gateway` | `https-wollbi` | `*.wollbi.ch`, the neighbourhood sites | `wollbi-gateway-tls` |
| `apps-gateway` | `ssh` | `*.ssh.wlkr.ch`, passthrough; see [SSH listener](<#ssh-listener>) | None here |
| `infra-gateway` | `https` | `*.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` | `infra-gateway-tls` |

A listener pins one hostname pattern and a wildcard certificate covers one zone, so a new domain is three files, never a name added to an existing listener:

1. A `Certificate` in `payload/platform/certificates/certificates.yaml`.
2. An HTTPS listener in `gateways.yaml` referencing it.
3. The zone in `domainFilters` in `payload/platform/external-dns/application.yaml`, or its routes are silently ignored.

The HTTPS listeners terminate TLS with cert-manager's wildcard certificates, so a new hostname needs no certificate of its own and nothing to renew. Each HTTPS listener pins its hostname pattern, so a route can only claim a name inside its Gateway's tree. A wildcard is a suffix match, so `*.k8s.wlkr.ch` still admits an `infra` name; such a route gets no traffic, because the infra names resolve to the other Gateway and the apps certificate covers one label only. Port 80 is accepted from all namespaces only so the central rule in `http-redirect.yaml` can send it to HTTPS. `apps-gateway` carries the annotation that makes [external-dns](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-dns/#configuration>) publish the router's public address instead of the Gateway's LAN one; the router forwards ports 80 and 443 to that LAN address.

`payload/platform/cilium/rbac-gateway-fix.yaml` grants the operator read access to Ingresses and IngressClasses: its Gateway API controller lists them too, and the chart grants that only with the Ingress controller enabled. Retry removing it on a chart major.

### Backend protocol

Envoy speaks HTTP/1.1 to every backend unless the Service port says otherwise: Cilium's `gatewayAPI.enableAppProtocol` makes it honour `appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c` and open HTTP/2 cleartext instead. A `GRPCRoute` needs that, because the Gateway translates gRPC-web into native gRPC, which only an HTTP/2 backend answers; Argo CD's `http2` port is the one user, see [Argo CD → CLI access](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/#cli-access>).

The CRDs arrive twice from one tag: `make install-cilium` applies the release bundle `standard-install.yaml` before ArgoCD exists, and the `gateway-api-crds` Application applies `config/crd/standard`, the directory that bundle is generated from. The Makefile reads the tag out of the Application, so the two cannot drift apart.

## Usage

Where the chart renders an `HTTPRoute` (Argo CD, OpenBao, Grafana), enable it in the values; a route only becomes a file of its own when it targets something the chart does not own, such as the Authentik outpost. Otherwise create an `HTTPRoute` in the app's namespace referencing the right Gateway; [external-dns](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-dns/index.md>) creates the record and the wildcard covers the name:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: Gateway
      name: apps-gateway
      namespace: kube-system
      sectionName: https
  hostnames:
    - "my-app.k8s.wlkr.ch"
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: my-app-svc
          port: 80
```

Use `infra-gateway` with a `*.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` hostname for platform tools, and the listener from the table above whose hostnames cover the name.

### SSH listener

The in-cluster Claude Code agents are reached over SSH tunnelled in TLS on port 443, the only port the router forwards to `apps-gateway`. Each agent's chart ships a `TLSRoute` for `<session>.ssh.wlkr.ch` pointing at its SSH Service.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `mode: Passthrough` | Cilium rejects a `TLS` listener in `Terminate` mode: the listener goes `Accepted=False` with "Using TLSRoute with TLS.mode Terminate is unsupported", and no route attaches. The Gateway forwards the stream by SNI and the agent pod ends the TLS with its own certificate |
| No `Certificate` here | A Secret cannot be referenced across namespaces, and a passthrough listener has no use for one. The chart requests one per session from `letsencrypt-prod` in the agent's namespace |
| `allowedRoutes.kinds: TLSRoute` | The listener serves nothing else, and `HTTPRoute`s cannot attach to it by accident |
| `TLSRoute` `v1` | Installed in the standard channel of the Gateway API CRDs; `v1alpha2` is no longer served. Cilium reads the CRD once at operator start, so after the CRDs change, restart `cilium-operator` |

DNS needs no record by hand: [external-dns](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-dns/#configuration>) reads the `TLSRoute` hostnames and publishes the router's public address, as for an `HTTPRoute`. A client connects with a TLS tunnel as its `ProxyCommand`, for example `openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h`.

Envoy checks its egress against the backend like any Gateway traffic, so the agents' namespace must admit the `ingress` entity on the SSH port; see [Security Policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/#network-policies>).

## Health check

Check that each HTTP listener carries only the redirect — `http` should show exactly `1`:

```bash
kubectl get gateway infra-gateway -n kube-system \
  -o jsonpath='{range .status.listeners[*]}{.name}={.attachedRoutes}{"\n"}{end}'
```

## Pitfalls

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Always set `sectionName`**
>
> A route that names no listener attaches to both, and on port 80 it beats the redirect: Gateway API resolves competing routes by hostname specificity, so a route naming a hostname wins over the catch-all redirect and serves the app in cleartext. Nothing reports it — every route is `Accepted`.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Nothing stops two apps claiming the same hostname**
>
> Both Gateways admit routes from every namespace, so a stray `HTTPRoute` can attach itself to either Gateway and claim a name inside its hostname pattern — see [Security Posture](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md>).

# GitHub runners

Linux jobs of a private repository run here instead of on GitHub's hosted runners, whose minutes a free organisation pays for. The [Actions Runner Controller](<https://github.com/actions/actions-runner-controller>) is two components: `arc-controller` runs the controller and its CRDs, `arc-runners` one scale set per repository. A job gets a fresh runner pod that exits when the job ends. macOS jobs cannot run here and stay on GitHub.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Scale sets | `homelab` and `homelab-wait` on `somuch-cloud/extractor.cafe` |
| Workflow label | `runs-on: homelab` |
| Depends on | [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) for the GitHub App in `kv/arc-runners/github-app` |
| If it is down | Jobs on `runs-on: homelab` queue on GitHub until a runner registers; nothing else notices |
| Health check | `kubectl -n arc-systems get pods` → the controller and one listener per scale set Running |
| Namespaces | `arc-systems` for the controller and the listeners, `arc-runners` for the runner pods, `arc-jobs` for the job pods the container hook starts |
| Files | `payload/platform/arc-controller/`, `payload/platform/arc-runners/`, and the three namespaces' files under `payload/platform/security/` |

## Configuration

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Controller and scale set chart on the same `targetRevision` | The controller deletes an `AutoscalingRunnerSet` whose chart version differs from its own, and Argo CD recreates it, in a loop; Renovate moves both in one PR |
| `githubConfigUrl` on the repository, not the organisation | No other repository in the organisation can schedule code onto the cluster |
| `githubConfigSecret: github-app` | A GitHub App rather than a PAT: no expiry and a token scoped to the installed repository — see [GitHub App](<#github-app>) |
| `controllerServiceAccount` spelled out | The chart finds the controller with Helm `lookup`, which Argo CD does not run |
| `minRunners` and `maxRunners` | No idle pods between pushes; the ceiling lets several pull requests run their parallel Linux jobs at once without queueing, while the requests stay a fraction of the workers' memory |
| `containerMode: kubernetes-novolume` | A job with `services:` or `container:` gets its own pod, started by the container hook through the API server. No privileged Docker daemon and no PVC per job. Where that pod runs, and with which token: [Job pods](<#job-pods>) |
| `ACTIONS_RUNNER_REQUIRE_JOB_CONTAINER: "false"` | A job without `container:` runs in the runner pod itself, as on a hosted runner |
| `arc-runners` and `arc-jobs` enforce `baseline` | The runner image uses `sudo`, and a service container such as PostgreSQL starts as root; neither passes `restricted` |
| `arc-jobs` is exempt from the user-namespace kill | buildah builds the images as root without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, which `baseline` forbids, so it re-executes itself in a user namespace; [Tetragon](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/tetragon/#enforcement>) records those instead of killing them, and its [alerts](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/tetragon/#policies>) leave out buildah's mounts and account-file writes and `go` running its test binaries in the job pods |
| The runner image as a full reference with a digest | Renovate tracks it; the chart passes the same image to the hook for the job pod's init container |
| `resources` | Unmeasured; the request fits a test suite with a database beside it, and the limit stops a runaway build before it starves the node |
| A second scale set, `homelab-wait`, for `ci-ok` alone | The wait holds its runner until every other check on the commit has finished; on the shared set, as many open pull requests as `maxRunners` fill it with waits and the checks they wait for never start. It runs no build, so it has no container mode and a small request |

### Job pods

The chart's own ServiceAccount for `kubernetes-novolume` may read every Secret in `arc-runners`, where the GitHub App key and each runner's JIT config live, and a step without `container:` runs in the runner pod with that token. The `homelab` set therefore runs its hook one namespace over.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `serviceAccountName: homelab-runner` | The chart then renders no Role of its own; `job-pods-rbac.yaml` grants the ServiceAccount rights in `arc-jobs` only |
| `ACTIONS_RUNNER_KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE: arc-jobs` | The hook creates the job pod and its environment Secret there, so the Secret verbs it needs reach nothing else |
| The Role is the hook's `requiredPermissions`, Secret `get` and `list` included | The hook checks every verb before each command and fails the job if one is missing; a step can still read the environment of another job running at the same time, from the same repository |
| `default` ServiceAccount in `arc-jobs` without a token | A job pod never calls the API server |

All jobs share `arc-jobs` and one Role, so a job can reach the pods and Secrets of any job running beside it. That is accepted because no repository with other contributors will use these runners; if that changes, it takes one scale set and namespace per trust level, each with its own Role.

### Controller

The `arc-controller` values, and why:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `flags.watchSingleNamespace: arc-runners` | The controller gets a Role in this namespace instead of a ClusterRole over every namespace |
| `logLevel: info`, `logFormat: json` | The chart's default is `debug`, which logs every reconcile; JSON is what Loki parses |
| Restricted security context on the controller and the listener | Both are distroless and run as non-root; the namespace enforces `baseline` and audits `restricted` |

### Metrics

`metrics` in the controller values turns on `/metrics` on port 8080 of the controller and of every listener it starts. The listener's are the scale set's view from GitHub (assigned jobs, desired, idle and registered runners, job start-up and run times), the controller's the runner pods it manages. Both PodMonitors in `payload/platform/arc-controller/podmonitors.yaml` set `honorLabels`, so the metrics keep their own `namespace`, the runners' namespace, instead of the pod's `arc-systems`.

The **GitHub Actions Runners** dashboard in `payload/platform/arc-controller/grafana-dashboards.yaml` reads them. The job metrics carry no scale set label, so its job panels take the scale set from the listener pod's name. Upstream's sample dashboard is not vendored: it filters on `actions_github_com_scale_set_name`, which this version does not export, and most of its panels stay empty.

### Network policy

Every rule in `arc-runners.yaml` and `arc-jobs.yaml` under `payload/platform/security/network-policies/`. Unlike the other namespaces, egress is every public address rather than a list of names.

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Ingress from the namespace and the node only | Runners and job pods serve nothing; the listener in `arc-systems` reaches GitHub, not the runners, and a runner reaches its job pod through the API server |
| Egress to the API server, `homelab` runner pods only | The container hook creates the job pod and execs each step into it; the `homelab-wait` runners run no hook, and job pods carry no token |
| Egress to `0.0.0.0/0` on 80 and 443, minus the private, carrier-grade and link-local ranges | A job downloads whatever its workflow names (actions, toolchains, packages), which no name list keeps up with. Cutting the private ranges keeps the LAN, the nodes and every in-cluster service out of reach |

The controller's and listeners' egress, GitHub's API and the Actions service only, and Prometheus' scrape of their metrics port, are in `payload/platform/security/network-policies/arc-systems.yaml`.

### GitHub App

One app per organisation, installed on each repository that has a scale set.

1. Create the app under the organisation's **Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App**: any name and homepage URL, **Webhook → Active** unticked, **Repository permissions → Administration: Read and write**, **Metadata: Read-only**, installable on this account only.
2. On the app's page, note the **App ID** and **Generate a private key**; the `.pem` file downloads.
3. **Install App** → **Only select repositories** → the repository. The installation ID is the number at the end of the installation's URL.
4. Store all three:

```bash
make bao-secrets    # answers the arc-runners/github-app prompts
```

1. Push the secret through and wait for the listener:

```bash
kubectl -n arc-runners annotate externalsecret github-app force-sync="$(date +%s)" --overwrite
kubectl -n arc-systems get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/component=runner-scale-set-listener
```

The scale set then appears under the repository's **Settings → Actions → Runners**.

## Usage

A job opts in with its label:

```yaml
runs-on: homelab
```

| Job shape | What runs where |
| --- | --- |
| Steps only | In the runner pod, on the runner image |
| `container:` | A job pod from that image; steps exec into it |
| `services:` | Needs a `container:` too; the services join the job pod and answer on `localhost` |

The runner image is GitHub's minimal [`actions-runner`](<https://github.com/actions/runner/blob/main/images/Dockerfile>), not the hosted `ubuntu-latest`: `git`, `curl`, `jq`, `unzip` and `sudo`, and no language toolchains. A job installs what it needs, pinned, or uses a `setup-*` action.

### Adding a scale set

1. Install the [GitHub App](<#github-app>) on the repository.
2. In `payload/platform/arc-runners/application.yaml`, copy a chart source with its own `helm.releaseName`, `githubConfigUrl` and `runnerScaleSetName`; a set that runs job pods keeps `containerMode`, `serviceAccountName` and `ACTIONS_RUNNER_KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE`.
3. In `job-pods-rbac.yaml`, a ServiceAccount, Role and binding for the set's hook, or `homelab-runner` again when the jobs share its trust level, see [Job pods](<#job-pods>).
4. In `payload/platform/security/network-policies/arc-runners.yaml`, the `container-hook` policy selects `actions.github.com/scale-set-name` `homelab` only; a set that runs a hook needs the same rule for its name.
5. A repository that runs `ci-ok` needs a `-wait` twin of the set, like `homelab-wait`, for the reason in [Configuration](<#configuration>).
6. Workflows opt in with `runs-on: <runnerScaleSetName>`.

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n arc-runners get autoscalingrunnerset,ephemeralrunner
kubectl -n arc-systems get pods
kubectl -n arc-systems logs -l app.kubernetes.io/component=runner-scale-set-listener --tail=50
```

A job waiting on `runs-on: homelab` with no runner pod in `arc-runners` means the listener is not getting it; its log and the controller's say why.

## Pitfalls

- **`Job Container is required.`** A job with `services:` and no `container:`. The hook runs services only beside a job container.
- **No Docker daemon.** The image carries the `docker` CLI, but nothing answers it: `docker build` and `docker run` steps fail.
- **No listener until the app is in OpenBao.** An empty `kv/arc-runners/github-app` syncs cleanly; the controller then fails to register the scale set with GitHub and says so in its log.
- **Removing a scale set takes the controller.** Its Roles carry the `actions.github.com/cleanup-protection` finalizer, which only the controller removes; take the scale set out first and let it go before touching `arc-controller`.

# Kured

[Kured](<https://kured.dev/>) applies the updates the nodes have staged. It watches every node for a sentinel file and, when it finds one, takes a cluster-wide lock, cordons and drains the node, reboots it and uncordons it when it is back. Flatcar's own `locksmithd` is masked because it reboots without draining, on a cluster where every node is a storage node.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kured` |
| Depends on | [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md>) for the alerts it gates on |
| If it is down | Nothing visible: staged OS and sysext updates simply never get applied |
| Health check | `kubectl -n kured logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=kured --tail=50` |
| Files | `payload/platform/kured/application.yaml` |

## Configuration

An update stages on disk and signals it by touching `/run/reboot-required`, Kured's default sentinel. `/run` is tmpfs, so the marker clears itself on reboot.

| Mechanism | Stages | Signals by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flatcar OS (update-engine) | New image on the passive A/B partition | `flatcar-reboot-sentinel.timer` |
| Kubernetes sysext | New `.raw` under `/opt/extensions/kubernetes` | `systemd-sysupdate` drop-in |

```
flowchart TD
    OS["update-engine<br/>OS image on the passive partition"] --> SEN
    KUBE["systemd-sysupdate<br/>kubernetes sysext"] --> SEN

    SEN["/run/reboot-required<br/>sentinel, on tmpfs"] --> TICK{"Kured checks<br/>every period"}

    TICK -->|"no sentinel"| SLEEP["Nothing to do until<br/>an update stages one"]
    TICK -->|"sentinel present"| ALERT{"Blocking alert firing?<br/>Ceph, etcd, node, API, Velero"}
    ALERT -->|"yes"| HELD["Reboot deferred while<br/>the cluster is unhealthy"]
    ALERT -->|"no"| LOCK{"Cluster lock free?"}
    LOCK -->|"another node<br/>is rebooting"| TAINT["Taint PreferNoSchedule,<br/>wait for the lock"]
    LOCK -->|"acquired"| DRAIN["Cordon and drain"]
    DRAIN -->|"drain fails"| GIVEUP["No reboot: uncordon,<br/>release the lock, retry"]
    DRAIN -->|"drained"| BOOT["systemctl reboot;<br/>new partition and<br/>sysexts take effect"]
    BOOT --> UP["Node comes back,<br/>sentinel gone with tmpfs"]
    UP --> DONE["Uncordon, drop the annotation,<br/>release the lock after a delay"]

    style SEN stroke-width:3px
```

The values are in `payload/platform/kured/application.yaml`; the reasoning:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| No reboot window | Kured acts as soon as it sees a sentinel; the guards below make that safe, not the clock |
| `concurrency` and `lockReleaseDelay` | One node down at a time. The rebooted node is uncordoned as soon as Kured's pod is back; the delay only holds the *next* node, long enough for the OSD to rejoin and the few minutes of backfill a reboot leaves, and as long as `CephOSDDown`'s `for`, so an OSD that did not come back is a firing alert before the next drain |
| `forceReboot: false` | A node that will not drain is a node worth looking at |
| `preferNoScheduleTaint` | A node pending reboot stops attracting pods about to be evicted again |
| `annotateNodes: true` | `kubectl get node -o yaml` shows why a node is cordoned |
| `VeleroBackupInProgress` on the alert list | Velero marks any backup it finds running at startup as Failed, and draining its node restarts it. The rule in `payload/platform/velero/application.yaml` compares attempts with outcomes per live Velero pod over a window longer than Velero's default limit on asynchronous operations; a backup that hangs drops out of the window, so it holds reboots for that long at most. A backup that starts in a Velero pod's first scrape interval has no zero sample to increase from and does not hold the gate. It routes to the `null` receiver because it fires every night |
| `alertFilterRegexp` with `alertFilterMatchOnly: true` | Kured asks Prometheus before taking a node down and refuses while any Ceph, etcd, node or API alert on the list fires. This is the automated "confirm Ceph has recovered" step from [Rebooting a node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md>): a second reboot during a backfill can take a placement group below its minimum replica count. Kured matches the alert name only, so Prometheus loads rules from [platform namespaces only](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/#scrape-targets>) |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The regex means the opposite of what it looks like**
>
> `alertFilterRegexp` normally lists alerts to **ignore**. With `alertFilterMatchOnly: true` these become the only alerts that block, because something is almost always firing in a homelab and blocking on any alert would mean never rebooting. An alert not on the list does not stop a reboot, so widen it if something turns out to matter — and read the flag twice before editing it. A name that no `PrometheusRule` defines blocks nothing and fails silently; the list once carried eight such names. Check every entry against the rules that exist, with the last command under [Health check](<#health-check>).

## Usage

To stop Kured rebooting anything without uninstalling it, take its cluster lock by hand; it holds until the annotation is removed. Clearing the sentinel does not work, because `flatcar-reboot-sentinel.timer` in `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2` re-touches it while an update is staged, and a DaemonSet cannot be scaled.

```bash
kubectl -n kured annotate ds kured weave.works/kured-node-lock='{"nodeID":"manual"}'
kubectl -n kured annotate ds kured weave.works/kured-node-lock-    # release it
```

To force a node to reboot on the next pass:

```bash
ssh core@<node> sudo touch /run/reboot-required
```

`NodeRebootPending` in `payload/platform/monitoring/node-update-rules.yaml` fires when the sentinel has been there for two days: Kured reboots one node at a time and refuses while Ceph or etcd is unhealthy, so a marker that old is a blocked node, not a queued one.

## Health check

```bash
# Which nodes want a reboot: kured_reboot_required is the sentinel's presence, per node
kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus 9090:9090 &
curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=kured_reboot_required == 1' \
  | jq -r '.data.result[].metric.node'

# Which node is being rebooted right now
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.annotations["weave.works/kured-reboot-in-progress"]) | .metadata.name'

# Whether a node has staged anything
ssh core@<node> 'ls -l /run/reboot-required; update_engine_client -status'

kubectl -n kured logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=kured --tail=50

# The alert names the gate may use: every entry in alertFilterRegexp must be here
kubectl get prometheusrule -A -o json | jq -r '.items[].spec.groups[].rules[] | select(.alert) | .alert' | sort -u | grep -E 'Ceph|etcd|KubeNode|KubeAPI|VeleroBackupInProgress'
```

# Logging

[Loki](<https://grafana.com/oss/loki/>) stores logs; [Grafana Alloy](<https://grafana.com/docs/alloy/latest/>) collects them. Both are queried from the existing Grafana at [monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch](<https://monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch>). Without them a crashed pod's logs are gone with the container, and on Flatcar the `kubelet`, `containerd`, `systemd-sysupdate` and `update-engine` logs live in journald and are reachable only over SSH to the node that is misbehaving.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `logging` |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) object storage for chunks, [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md>) for the Grafana that queries it |
| If it is down | Logs stop being collected and are not backfilled. The [audit log](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>) loses its durable copy, and the [log alerts](<#alerting>) stop |
| Health check | `kubectl -n logging get pods`, then a `{job="kubernetes-audit"}` query in Grafana |
| Metrics | Loki and Alloy, each through its chart's `ServiceMonitor`; both sets of dashboards are listed under [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/#dashboards>) |
| Files | `payload/platform/loki/` and `payload/platform/alloy/`, one chart Application each (`loki`, `alloy`); `payload/platform/logging/`, the `logging` Application: the bucket claim in `bucket.yaml`, `loki-rules.yaml`, the Grafana datasource and the Alloy dashboards |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Not Promtail, and not the `grafana/loki` chart**
>
> Promtail reached end of life in March 2026; Alloy is its supported replacement. Loki comes from `grafana-community/loki`: the OSS chart moved to [grafana-community/helm-charts](<https://github.com/grafana-community/helm-charts>) in March 2026, and what stayed in `grafana/loki` is maintained for Grafana Enterprise Logs customers, pins a `k8s-sidecar` several minor releases behind and closes open-source pull requests with a pointer to the community repository.

## Configuration

### Sources

| Source | Path | Labels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container logs | `/var/log/pods/<ns>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/*.log` | `namespace`, `pod`, `container`, `node`, `app` |
| Node journal | `/var/log/journal` | `unit`, `node`, `job="systemd-journal"` |
| API server audit log | `/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log` | `verb`, `audit_level`, `node`, `job="kubernetes-audit"` |
| Hubble policy verdicts | `/var/run/cilium/hubble/events.log` | `verdict`, `node`, `job="hubble"` |

The first three are on the root filesystem, so one `varlog: true` mount covers them; the Hubble export is a separate read-only hostPath — see [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/#configuration>). The audit log exists only on the control-plane nodes; Alloy runs everywhere and `local.file_match` finds nothing on the workers. Audit events keep only `verb` and `audit_level` as labels — small closed sets — while user and resource stay in the line where `| json` can reach them. See [Audit logging](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>) for what is recorded.

### Alloy pipeline

| Stage | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `discovery.kubernetes` with a `spec.nodeName` field selector | Each agent discovers only its own node's pods; without it every agent watches every pod and discards all but its own |
| `stage.cri {}` on container logs | containerd writes `<timestamp> <stream> <flags> <message>`; without it the timestamp lands inside the line and Loki stamps everything at ingest time |
| `discovery.relabel "journal"` sets `job` | `loki.source.journal` overwrites `job` with its component ID after applying `labels`; only relabel rules run after that |
| `stage.json`, `stage.labels`, `stage.timestamp` on audit events | Stamps each event with its `requestReceivedTimestamp` rather than when Alloy read the file |

| Setting in `alloy/application.yaml` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Control-plane toleration | Without it Alloy runs on the workers alone and neither the audit log nor the control-plane kubelets' journals reach Loki |
| `enableReporting: false` | Alloy otherwise sends usage statistics to `stats.grafana.org`; the policy audit showed the call, and telemetry is off in every component here |
| `runAsUser: 0` | The log files are root-owned; a non-root Alloy does not fail, it silently collects nothing. Read-only root, no capabilities and `RuntimeDefault` seccomp lock the rest down |
| `emptyDir` at `/tmp` | The chart's `storagePath` defaults to `/tmp/alloy`, unwritable on a read-only root; it holds tailing positions, which did not survive a restart before either |
| `rbac.rules` without `secrets` | The chart's ClusterRole reads every Secret for `remote.kubernetes.secret`, which nothing here uses; [`KubernetesAuditSecretReadByUser`](<#alerting>) would show such a read, but a grant with no purpose is better not made |

### Storage

Loki runs as a single binary (`deploymentMode: Monolithic`) and keeps chunks in the [Ceph object store](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/#object-storage>); a local PVC on `rook-ceph-block` holds the WAL and the index being built. The bucket is the `ObjectBucketClaim` in `logging/bucket.yaml`, with a fixed `bucketName`: a generated name carries a random suffix that would have to be read back at runtime, a fixed one keeps Loki's config static and identical after a rebuild.

| Setting in `loki/application.yaml` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `singleBinary.extraArgs` `-config.expand-env=true` and `singleBinary.extraEnvFrom` | Rook writes the bucket credentials to a Secret, Loki reads them as `${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}` — nothing in Git |
| `loki.analytics.reporting_enabled: false` | Loki otherwise sends usage statistics to `stats.grafana.org` a few times a day; same reason as Alloy's switch above |
| `chunksCache` and `resultsCache` off | Four memcached pods in front of a Loki this size |
| `loki.podSecurityContext` | Adds `RuntimeDefault` seccomp at pod level, covering the rules sidecar too |
| Retention with the compactor enabled | Old chunks are actually deleted |
| `rulerConfig` | The ruler evaluates LogQL alerts and posts them to Alertmanager; without it the audit log and the journal are query-only. Rules come from local files the chart's sidecar copies out of `loki_rule` ConfigMaps, so `storage.type` is `local` rather than the bucket the chart would pick; `rule_path` is the ruler's scratch directory and must not be the rules directory |
| `rbac.namespaced: true` and `sidecar.rules.resource: configmap` | The rules are ConfigMaps in `logging`, so a Role there replaces the chart's cluster-wide ClusterRole, for the same reason as Alloy's `rbac.rules` above; the chart's binding could not be repointed because a `roleRef` is immutable. `resource: configmap` keeps the sidecar from listing Secrets |
| `retention_stream` for the `findings-history` container | The daily [Trivy summary](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/trivy-operator/#history>) is a few lines and the only long-range record of findings, so that one stream outlives the general `retention_period` by far |

### Alerting

Alerts over logs live in `logging/loki-rules.yaml`, a ConfigMap labelled `loki_rule` in the same format as a `PrometheusRule` group with LogQL expressions. The `k8s-sidecar-target-directory: fake` annotation puts the file under the tenant directory the ruler reads (`fake` is the tenant when `auth_enabled` is off). Prometheus-side rules stay with their components; these are the events only a log carries. Loki's own health alerts (request errors, latency, panics, the compactor) are the chart's `monitoring.alerts`, the mixin Grafana maintains, not rules written here.

| Alert | Fires on | Why it is a log alert |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `KubernetesAuditExecIntoPod` | A successful `exec` or `attach` | Only the [audit log](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>) records who ran what in which pod |
| `KubernetesAuditSecretReadByUser` | A Secret read by a person, or by a ServiceAccount outside its own namespace that is not on the allowlist of platform controllers | A stolen token reads across namespaces; the allowlist is the ServiceAccounts RBAC grants Secrets to cluster-wide, plus the runner's in `arc-jobs` only, where its [container hook](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/#job-pods>) keeps each job's environment, and a ServiceAccount reading its own namespace is what its Role is for |
| `KubernetesAuditRbacBindingChanged` | A ClusterRole or ClusterRoleBinding written by anything but the ArgoCD controller or a `kube-system` controller | Argo CD is the only intended writer; namespaced RoleBindings are left out because CloudNativePG reconciles one per database continuously |
| `KubernetesAuditForbiddenBurst` | More than ten 403s from one identity in ten minutes | What RBAC probing from a compromised pod looks like |
| `KubernetesAuditAnonymousRequest` | A successful anonymous request | The audit policy drops the health endpoints, the only legitimate anonymous paths |
| `KubernetesAuditEsoTokenMinted` | A successful `serviceaccounts/token` create for an `external-secrets-vault` ServiceAccount by anyone but ESO's controller, a kubelet starting a pod under that ServiceAccount included | OpenBao records the same role and ServiceAccount whoever minted the token, so only the audit log names the minter. A stolen controller token or a legacy token Secret does not trip it: neither shows a different user on this request |
| `OpenBaoSecretReadOutsideEso` | A `kv/data/` read from OpenBao by any token whose display name is not `kubernetes-<namespace>-external-secrets-vault`, ESO's login for one of its [stores](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#kubernetes-auth>) | [OpenBao's audit device](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#audit-devices>) writes to stdout; ESO is the only day-to-day reader, every Kubernetes role is bound to that ServiceAccount name, and a token created by hand is prefixed `token-`, so it cannot borrow the name |
| `TetragonSudoInContainer` | `sudo` executed in a container, except the `smartctl` and `nvme` calls `ceph-osd` makes once a day for its device health report | Only the exec event carries the binary and its parent |
| `TetragonPrivilegedExec` | A setuid, setgid or file-capability binary raised privileges on exec, with the same `ceph-osd` exception | The `binary_properties` field exists only in the exec event |
| `TetragonFilelessExec` | A binary executed from memory, via `memfd_create` or an anonymous descriptor, except runc's sealed self-copy on every `exec` | Same |
| `TetragonDeletedBinaryExec` | A binary executed after its last link was removed | Same; see [Tetragon](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/tetragon/#policies>) |
| `TetragonUnsignedKernelModule` | A kernel module loaded without a valid signature, on a node or from a container | The signature result is an argument of the kprobe event, not a metric label |
| `HubblePolicyDrops` | More than three `POLICY_DENIED` packets in ten minutes for one source workload, destination and port, each counted once although Hubble also reports it as a policy verdict; replies, ICMP errors (a pod's port-unreachable answer to a DNS reply that came too late), pods still in the `init` identity and addresses with no pod behind them are left out. The `namespace` label is the policy that refused, so the mail names the file to edit | A connection's retransmits pass the threshold and a name rule's single early `SYN` does not; the metric counts per namespace pair only and misses the first burst of a new pair |
| `NodeSshLogin` | An accepted SSH login on a node | Nothing routine logs in after provisioning |
| `NodeSshAuthFailures` | More than five failed SSH attempts on a node in ten minutes | Password authentication is off; repeats are a scan or a retried key |

To confirm the ruler loaded a rule:

```bash
kubectl -n logging port-forward svc/loki 3100:3100
curl -s localhost:3100/loki/api/v1/rules
```

### Dashboards

`grafana-dashboards.yaml` carries three dashboards from the Alloy mixin (`operations/alloy-mixin/rendered/dashboards/`), unmodified; the chart renders none and Renovate does not see the copy, so re-copy them when Alloy moves a minor version. The mixin's other dashboards cover features this Alloy does not use. The Loki datasource in `grafana-datasource.yaml` declares its namespace as `monitoring`, the only namespace the Grafana sidecar watches for `grafana_datasource` ConfigMaps.

## Usage

Choose **Loki** as the datasource in Grafana and query by label:

```text
{namespace="rook-ceph"} |= "error"
{unit="kubelet.service", node="odin"}
{namespace="openbao"} |= "sealed"
{job="kubernetes-audit"} | json | objectRef_resource="secrets"
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n logging get pods
```
