Then run a `{job="kubernetes-audit"}` query in Grafana; an empty result with healthy pods means the control-plane agents are not reading the file.

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Loki settings belong on `singleBinary`, not `global`**
>
> `global.extraArgs` and `global.extraEnvFrom` look right, but the single-binary StatefulSet reads only `singleBinary.extraArgs` and `singleBinary.extraEnvFrom`. Set globally, the config is full of unexpanded `${...}` and Loki cannot authenticate to RGW, with an error pointing nowhere near the cause. Likewise `singleBinary.podSecurityContext` does not exist and is silently inert.

# metrics-server

[metrics-server](<https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server>) serves the `metrics.k8s.io` API that `kubectl top`, every `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` and the [descheduler](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/descheduler/index.md>) read; the scheduler does not, it places on requests. Without it `kubectl top` errors and an HPA sits at `<unknown>/<target>` with no logs, events or clue. Prometheus is not a substitute: it answers PromQL from its own store, while the resource metrics API is an aggregated Kubernetes API that core controllers read directly.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system`; kubelet-csr-approver in `kubelet-csr-approver` |
| Depends on | kubelet-csr-approver, or the kubelet certificates it verifies are never issued; [cert-manager](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md>) for its own serving certificate |
| If it is down | `kubectl top`, every HPA and the [descheduler](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/descheduler/index.md>)'s node usage. Nothing else notices |
| Health check | `kubectl top nodes` → a row per node |
| Files | `payload/platform/metrics-server/`, `payload/platform/kubelet-csr-approver/` |

## Configuration

### Verifying the kubelet instead of trusting it

A kubelet serves a self-signed certificate by default, so the usual shortcut is `--kubelet-insecure-tls`, which makes the metrics path spoofable by anything that can occupy a kubelet's address. Kubernetes deliberately does not auto-approve `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` CSRs, since a compromised node could request a certificate for any name, so doing it properly takes three pieces:

| Piece | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `serverTLSBootstrap: true` | `ansible/templates/kubeadm.yaml.j2` | The kubelet requests a serving certificate from the cluster CA |
| [kubelet-csr-approver](<https://github.com/postfinance/kubelet-csr-approver>) | `payload/platform/kubelet-csr-approver/application.yaml` | Approves those CSRs, constrained by `providerRegex` (only the inventory's node names; anything else is **denied**), `providerIpPrefixes` (the nodes' subnet), a one-day `maxExpirationSeconds`, and `bypassDnsResolution` because node names come from the Ansible inventory, not a resolver |
| `--kubelet-certificate-authority` | `payload/platform/metrics-server/application.yaml` | metrics-server verifies against the cluster CA |

| Setting in `metrics-server/application.yaml` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Flags via `defaultArgs`, not `args` | The default list already sets `--kubelet-preferred-address-types`, and a flag passed twice leaves the winner to parsing order. It is `InternalIP` because node hostnames do not resolve here |
| Two replicas and a PodDisruptionBudget | A node reboot does not take the resource metrics API down |
| `tls.type: cert-manager` with `apiService.insecureSkipTLSVerify: false` | The other half of the path: the chart's self-signed `Issuer` signs the serving certificate and the cainjector copies its CA into the `APIService`, so kube-apiserver verifies metrics-server instead of trusting whatever answers at the Service |

## Health check

```bash
kubectl get csr | grep kubelet-serving   # should be Approved,Issued
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io   # Available True, caBundle filled
kubectl top nodes
```

`Pending` CSRs mean kubelet-csr-approver is not running or a node name does not match the regex. `Denied` means the regex or the IP prefix is wrong — check the controller's logs before widening either.

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Adding a node means editing the regex**
>
> A node missing from `providerRegex` has its CSR denied, keeps its self-signed certificate, and silently goes missing from `kubectl top`. Add it to the regex when you add it to the inventory.

# Monitoring

Full observability stack based on [kube-prometheus-stack](<https://github.com/prometheus-community/helm-charts/tree/main/charts/kube-prometheus-stack>): Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, node-exporter and kube-state-metrics. node-exporter runs in its own `node-exporter` namespace so that only it is admitted at the `privileged` level ([security policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/#pod-security-admission>)). The chart's default rule set is good; its default routing swallows every alert, which is what most of this page is about.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `monitoring` |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for Prometheus and Grafana volumes, [Authentik](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md>) for the Grafana login |
| If it is down | No alerts and no metrics — and [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) loses the alert gate it checks before rebooting a node |
| Health check | `kubectl -n monitoring get prometheus,alertmanager`; the `Watchdog` alert should always be firing |
| UI | `monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` (Grafana), `prometheus.` and `alertmanager.` |
| Files | `payload/platform/monitoring/`, `payload/platform/prometheus-operator-crds/` |

## Configuration

### CRDs

The `monitoring.coreos.com` CRDs are a separate `prometheus-operator-crds` Application, from the prometheus-community chart of that name, and this chart runs with `crds.enabled: false`. Cilium, cert-manager, External Secrets, Rook and OpenBao all render ServiceMonitors or PrometheusRules, and a missing kind fails their sync until the CRDs exist — see [Bootstrap convergence](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/#bootstrap-convergence>). The Application has no resources finalizer, so deleting it leaves the CRDs, and every ServiceMonitor, Prometheus and Alertmanager with them, in place.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Two versions that have to agree**
>
> `prometheus-operator-crds` must carry the same operator version as kube-prometheus-stack; an operator newer than its CRDs can depend on fields they do not define. Renovate bumps them separately: merge the CRD bump first, or both together — see [Maintenance](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/maintenance/index.md>).

### Alerting

Alertmanager routes to email. The chart's `config` is off (`alertmanagerSpec.useExistingSecret`) and `alertmanager-config.yaml` renders the whole `alertmanager.yaml` through ESO into `alertmanagerSpec.configSecret`, because only the password has a file form (`smtp_auth_password_file`) and the login and recipient are e-mail addresses that do not belong in Git.

| Setting in `alertmanager-config.yaml` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `smtp_smarthost` on port 465 | Implicit TLS, which Alertmanager selects from the port; `smtp_require_tls` stays on so a move back to 587 cannot fall to plaintext |
| `smtp_from` equals the login | mailbox.org refuses a sender the login does not own |
| Grouping by `namespace`, with `group_interval` and `repeat_interval` in hours and a shorter pair for `critical`; resolved notifications sent | mailbox.org caps what an account may send. One mail per alert and namespace came to hundreds a day once a node was down, the account was refused from then on, and the critical mails went unsent with the rest. A namespace's alerts usually share a cause, so one mail lists them together |
| `Watchdog` routed to `null` | It fires continuously as proof the pipeline is alive; mailing it would train the recipient to filter the sender |
| `VeleroBackupInProgress` routed to `null` | It fires for every nightly backup as [Kured's gate](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/#configuration>), not as a problem |
| `KubeJobFailed` disabled in the chart (`defaultRules.disabled`) and redefined in `job-rules.yaml`, bound to Jobs started in the last day | The chart's rule fires for as long as a failed Job object exists, so one old failure reads as an outage for weeks. Failed Jobs carry no failure time, so the bound counts from the start |
| Inhibit rules repeated from the chart defaults | A supplied config replaces the whole document, so nothing is inherited |
| Every templated value through `toJson` | A password containing `:`, `#` or a quote cannot break the rendered file |
| `externalUrl` on both `prometheusSpec` and `alertmanagerSpec` in `application.yaml` | The "Source" and Alertmanager links in a mail are built from these; unset, they point at the in-cluster Service, which nothing outside the cluster can open |

The three values come from `kv/monitoring/smtp` (`username`, `password`, `to`); `make bao-secrets` prompts for them, or by hand:

```bash
bao kv put kv/monitoring/smtp username=... password=... to=...
```

For another provider, change `smtp_smarthost` in the template and the three values in OpenBao.

### Scrape targets

Every `ServiceMonitor` and `PodMonitor` in every namespace, through the five `*SelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false` settings: the chart treats an empty selector as unset and renders `release: kube-prometheus-stack` in its place, which limits Prometheus to its own targets.

`PrometheusRule`s load only from the namespaces the `apps` project cannot deploy to, matched on the `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label the API server sets. [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/#configuration>) gates reboots on alert names, so a workload's rule named `CephHealthError` would otherwise stop OS updates cluster-wide. A rule in a new platform namespace loads only once that namespace is on the list in `ruleNamespaceSelector`.

| Target | Made scrapable by | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager | A per-node `bind-address` patch in `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2` (kubeadm binds them to `127.0.0.1`) | HTTPS with a self-signed certificate, so the ServiceMonitors set `insecureSkipVerify`; the ServiceAccount token still authenticates |
| etcd | A per-node `listen-metrics-urls` patch in the same template (kubeadm listens on `127.0.0.1` only) | Plain HTTP on 2381, serving only `/metrics` and `/health`; client and peer APIs stay on mTLS |
| Ceph | `monitoring.enabled` on the `CephCluster` — see [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/#monitoring>) |  |
| kube-proxy | Not scraped (`kubeProxy.enabled: false`) | Cilium replaces it; the default would keep `KubeProxyDown` firing forever |
| CRD status fields: CloudNativePG's ObjectStores and Backups | kube-state-metrics' `customResourceState` config in the chart values, one `rbac.extraRules` entry per kind | A `StateSet` per enum field and a `Gauge` per timestamp, no more; the rule that reads a kind sits with its component, and the namespace it lives in has to be on the rule list above |
| Pod labels: OpenBao's `openbao-sealed` | kube-state-metrics' `metricLabelsAllowlist` in the chart values | Exported as `label_<name>` on `kube_pod_labels`; only listed labels, since every one adds a series per pod |

> [!NOTE]
>
> A cluster provisioned before the kubeadm change keeps the old flags in its static pod manifests; until those nodes are reprovisioned the three control-plane targets stay down.

### Grafana

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `disable_login_form` and `oauth_auto_login` | Opening the URL bounces straight to Authentik and back; `role_attribute_path` with `role_attribute_strict` maps the three Grafana groups and refuses everyone else, see [Groups and roles](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/#groups-and-roles>) |
| `analytics.*` off and `disable_gravatar` | Grafana otherwise reports usage to Grafana Labs, asks grafana.com for updates and fetches every user's avatar from Gravatar; the Grafana network policy names none of those and the policy audit showed the Gravatar call. Telemetry is off in every component here |
| `grafana-oidc.yaml` | The OIDC client is generated into OpenBao and read by both sides — see [Authentik](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/#client-secrets>) |
| `grafana.route.main` | The chart renders Grafana's `HTTPRoute`. Prometheus and Alertmanager stay in `httproute.yaml`: their routes point at Authentik's outpost, which no chart template can express |
| `grafana.admin.existingSecret`, from `grafana-admin.yaml` | Left unset, the chart generates a new password on every render, so the Secret is always OutOfSync and `checksum/secret` restarts Grafana on every sync. The admin account is the [break-glass path](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/#when-authentik-is-down>); never set `grafana.adminPassword` in Git |
| `grafana.rbac.create: false` with `grafana-sidecar-rbac.yaml`, and `sidecar.*.resource: configmap` | Dashboards and datasources are ConfigMaps, so an own ClusterRole and binding grant those alone instead of the chart's ConfigMaps-and-Secrets pair, for the reason given with [Alloy's `rbac.rules`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/#alloy-pipeline>); the chart's binding is dropped rather than repointed because a `roleRef` is immutable |
| `Recreate` strategy | The dashboard PVC is RWO; under `RollingUpdate` the new pod waits for a volume the old pod releases only once the new one is Ready, parking on `FailedAttachVolume` |
| Prometheus and Grafana memory limits well above their requests | Both grow with series count and dashboard load, and OOMKilling the thing that reports cluster health is the failure worth avoiding; the limit is a ceiling for a runaway, sized by the [2.5x-peak rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/#components>), not a budget |
| Prometheus `retention` and `retentionSize` | Whichever is hit first wins. The size cap is the floor under the volume: a series count that grows faster than planned drops the oldest blocks instead of filling the disk and crashlooping Prometheus |
| Alertmanager `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, on the ServiceAccount and in `alertmanagerSpec` | Nothing binds a role to it — the operator talks to the API — so the token would only be a credential in a pod reachable from the Gateway. The operator sets the pod field itself, so the account's setting alone changes nothing |

### Dashboards

Where a chart can render a dashboard, it does; only charts without one get a vendored copy, which Renovate does not update — the header of each file names its upstream tag.

| Component | Dashboards | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md>) | Cilium Metrics, Cilium Operator, four Hubble dashboards | Chart: `dashboards`, `operator.dashboards`, `hubble.metrics.dashboards` |
| [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) | OpenBao | Chart: `serverTelemetry.grafanaDashboard` |
| [External Secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md>) | External Secrets Operator | Chart: `grafanaDashboard` |
| [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) | Ceph Cluster, Ceph - OSD (Single), Ceph - Pools | Vendored: `rook-ceph/grafana-dashboards.yaml` |
| [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) | Alloy / Controller, Alloy / Loki Components, Alloy / Resources | Vendored: `logging/grafana-dashboards.yaml` |
| [Loki](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) | The Loki mixin: Reads, Writes, Operational, Chunks, Retention and the rest | Chart: `monitoring.dashboards`, with `monitoring.rules` for the recording rules they read |
| ArgoCD | ArgoCD | Vendored: `argocd-config/grafana-dashboards.yaml` |
| [Tetragon](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/tetragon/index.md>) | Tetragon | Written for this cluster: `tetragon/grafana-dashboards.yaml`; upstream ships none |
| [GitHub runners](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/index.md>) | GitHub Actions Runners | Written for this cluster: `arc-controller/grafana-dashboards.yaml`; upstream's sample filters on labels ARC 0.15 does not export |
| [Trivy Operator](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/trivy-operator/index.md>) | Trivy Operator | Written for this cluster: `trivy-operator/grafana-dashboards.yaml` |

## Usage

### Adding a dashboard

Add a ConfigMap labelled `grafana_dashboard: "1"` next to the component it describes, in a file named `grafana-dashboards.yaml` and a ConfigMap named `<component>-grafana-dashboards`; a Secret carrying the label is not read. The sidecar watches only the platform namespaces listed in `sidecar.dashboards.searchNamespace`, so a workload cannot replace a dashboard; a component in a new namespace adds it there, and the `apps` project must not be able to deploy to it. Prefer the chart's own dashboard where it has one. A dashboard built in the UI survives restarts on the PVC but lives nowhere else: not in Git, not on a rebuilt cluster.

### Growing the Prometheus volume

Kubernetes cannot expand a StatefulSet's `volumeClaimTemplate`, so raising the request in `payload/platform/monitoring/application.yaml` does not resize the claim that already exists. The operator handles its own half of that: it fails the StatefulSet update on the immutable field, logs `recreating StatefulSet because the update operation wasn't possible`, and rebuilds it orphaned so the pod survives. Only the claim is left behind.

1. Merge the size bump and wait for the Application to sync.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n argocd get app kube-prometheus-stack -o jsonpath='{.status.sync.status}'
   ```
2. Patch the claim to the same size. This is the one step nothing automates.

   ```bash
   SIZE=$(awk '/prometheusSpec:/{f=1} f&&/storage: /{print $2; exit}' \
     payload/platform/monitoring/application.yaml)
   kubectl -n monitoring patch pvc \
     prometheus-kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus-db-prometheus-kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus-0 \
     --patch "{\"spec\": {\"resources\": {\"requests\": {\"storage\": \"$SIZE\"}}}}"
   ```
3. The claim parks on `FileSystemResizePending` and the filesystem grows when the volume is next mounted, so the pod is restarted and Prometheus replays its WAL — a scrape gap of about a minute, not a seamless resize. Wait for the claim to report the new capacity.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n monitoring get pvc -w \
     -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CAP:.status.capacity.storage
   ```

If the operator has not rebuilt the StatefulSet within a sync interval, do it by hand; `--cascade=orphan` keeps the pod and the claim.

```bash
kubectl -n monitoring delete statefulset \
  -l operator.prometheus.io/name=kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus --cascade=orphan
```

Alertmanager and Grafana take the same two steps, with their own claim names.

### Resetting the Grafana admin password

Grafana reads the password only when it creates its database, so changing `kv/monitoring/grafana-admin` later does not change what it checks. Reset it to the value in OpenBao rather than a new one: `grafana-admin.yaml` pushes the generated password with `updatePolicy: IfNotExists`, so OpenBao keeps the first value forever and a rebuilt Grafana starts from it.

```bash
PASSWORD=$(kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- \
  bao kv get -mount=kv -field=password monitoring/grafana-admin)
kubectl -n monitoring exec deploy/kube-prometheus-stack-grafana -c grafana -- \
  grafana cli admin reset-admin-password "$PASSWORD"
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheus,alertmanager
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheus kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceMonitorSelector}'   # should print {}
kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/kube-prometheus-stack-alertmanager 9093:9093
# then open http://localhost:9093 and check Status -> Config
```

`Watchdog` proves the pipeline as far as Alertmanager and not one step further; SMTP auth, spam heuristics and an expired password are unmonitored. Send yourself a test alert once and confirm it arrives.

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Prometheus is a single replica, Alertmanager is not**
>
> Alertmanager runs two replicas spread over the workers with a PDB that lets one go, so a [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) drain keeps alerting up. A second Prometheus would double the memory limit and the volume in `application.yaml`, which the [2.5x-peak rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/#components>) leaves no room for on a worker, so it stays single: its node's drain loses metrics for the restart, and Kured's alert gate fails closed until it is back.

# OpenBao

[OpenBao](<https://openbao.org/>) is the cluster's secret store, an open-source fork of HashiCorp Vault. It holds every secret the cluster consumes, surfaced as native `Secret` objects by the [External Secrets Operator](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md>). Sealed, nothing that needs a credential works, and the failure looks like six unrelated things breaking at once.

```
flowchart LR
    Operator([Operator]) -->|bao CLI| Bao[(OpenBao<br/>KV v2)]
    ESO[External Secrets<br/>Operator] -->|read, write once| Bao
    ESO -->|create/update| KSecret[K8s Secret]
    App[App Pod] -->|env / volume| KSecret

    style Bao fill:#e1f5ff,stroke:#0288d1
```

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `openbao` |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for its Raft volumes. A fresh bootstrap [pauses here](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/#bootstrap-pauses-at-openbao>) until OpenBao is initialised and unsealed |
| Seal | Shamir, unsealed by hand; the share count and threshold are set in `scripts/bao-init.sh` |
| If it is down — or merely sealed | No `ExternalSecret` resolves, so cert-manager cannot renew and pods that mount a materialised Secret will not start. It looks healthy from the outside |
| Health check | `bao status` on every pod → `Sealed: false`; see [Health check](<#health-check>) |
| UI | `vault.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` — the one platform UI *not* behind Authentik, deliberately |
| Files | `payload/platform/openbao/` |

## Configuration

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Mode | HA, integrated Raft on a Ceph PVC per replica; the replica count is in `application.yaml` |
| Audit storage | Separate PVC on `rook-ceph-block`, written by the `file` audit device — see [Audit devices](<#audit-devices>) |
| TLS | Terminates at the Gateway; plain HTTP at `http://openbao.openbao.svc.cluster.local:8200` |
| Chart | Upstream [`openbao/openbao-helm`](<https://github.com/openbao/openbao-helm>), pinned in `application.yaml` |

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Pod security context restated in full | The chart's `securityContext.pod` and `.container` replace rather than merge, so a block that names only what differs loses the rest. The image's `USER` is a name, so without the numeric IDs the kubelet refuses the container as unprovably non-root — on pod recreation, typically after a reboot. The full block is what lets the namespace enforce `restricted` ([security policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/#pod-security-admission>)) |
| `image.repository` without a registry | The chart prepends `server.image.registry` (`quay.io`) itself |
| `unauthenticated_metrics_access` | `/v1/sys/metrics` otherwise wants a token the ServiceMonitor does not have. The metrics carry counts and timings, not paths or secrets, and only the namespace policy's callers and the Gateway reach port 8200 |
| `retry_join` stanzas | `bao operator init` initialises one Raft cluster on one pod; these make the other replicas join it as they start. `service_registration "kubernetes"` only labels pods `active` and `standby` |
| `serverTelemetry.grafanaDashboard` | Renders OpenBao's upstream dashboard (grafana.com 23725) |
| `server.gateway.httpRoute` | The chart renders the UI's `HTTPRoute`, to the `active` Service so the browser never lands on a standby; the chart's warning about terminating TLS before the server concerns certificate authentication, which nothing here uses |

### Audit devices

Two, declared as `audit` stanzas in the server config in `application.yaml` (this OpenBao refuses `bao audit enable` over the API): a `file` device on the audit PVC, and a second `file` device on `stdout`, which [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) ships to Loki with the rest of the container's output. Without one, who read which secret is recorded nowhere; with only one, a full PVC would make OpenBao refuse every request, because a request no enabled device can log is refused. Values are HMACed in both; paths and identities are not. The config is read at start-up, and the StatefulSet updates `OnDelete`, so a change lands when each pod next restarts — see [Unsealing after a restart](<#unsealing-after-a-restart>).

`OpenBaoSecretReadOutsideEso` in [`loki-rules.yaml`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/#alerting>) fires on a `kv/data/` read by anything but the External Secrets Operator's roles: the operator, a generated root token, or a token that should not exist. A standby audits a request before it resolves the token, so its `please forward to the active node` rejections carry no identity; the rule drops them, and every `ClusterSecretStore` targets the `openbao-active` Service so ESO never produces one.

```text
{namespace="openbao", container="openbao"} |= `"type":"response"` |= `kv/data/` | json | __error__=""
```

### KV layout

One KV v2 engine at `kv/`; every leaf is `<workload>/<purpose>`, where a workload's prefix is its namespace, the only one [its store](<#kubernetes-auth>) reaches. ExternalSecrets reference `cert-manager/route53` without the `data/` prefix ESO adds itself. A path is written by exactly one of two things: a `PushSecret` beside the `ExternalSecret` that reads it, when every value is random — see [Generated secrets](<#generated-secrets>) — or `make bao-secrets` (an agent session's PAT: `make claude-session-pat`), when a value belongs to an account outside the cluster. A path never mixes the two, because a `bao kv put` replaces the whole path.

| Path | Keys | Read by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `authentik/config` (generated) | `secret-key`, `bootstrap-password`, the ArgoCD and Grafana client id/secret pairs | Authentik, ArgoCD and Grafana — generating the OIDC credentials up front keeps both sides of each integration declarative |
| `cert-manager/route53` | `access-key-id`, `secret-access-key` | The `certificates` Application |
| `external-dns/route53` | `access-key-id`, `secret-access-key` | external-dns |
| `monitoring/grafana-admin` (generated) | `password` | Grafana |
| `monitoring/smtp` | `username`, `password`, `to` | Alertmanager |
| `kneadtime/config` | `vapid-private-key` | The Knead Time reminder service — a P-256 key in PEM that signs every push; rotating it retires every subscription taken with the old one |
| `claude-agents/argocd` | `token` | The agents' Argo CD API token — [Agent account](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/#agent-account>); empty until generated |
| `shot-bridge/accounts` | `lm-username`, `lm-password`, `apns-key-id`, `apns-key-p8` | The Shot Timer bridge's La Marzocco login and APNs key — [Shot Timer bridge](<https://homelab-apps.wlkr.ch/shot-bridge/#secrets>); the APNs keys are empty until the key is created |
| `arc-runners/github-app` | `app-id`, `installation-id`, `private-key` | The GitHub App the Actions runners register with — [GitHub runners](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/#github-app>); empty until the app is created |
| `claude-<session>/github` | `token` | One agent session's GitHub PAT, for any session name: `make claude-session-pat SESSION=<session>` stores it, adding `DELETE=1` removes the path. Not part of `make bao-secrets`, so a session needs no platform change. Empty until typed in |
| `velero/repository` (generated) | `password` | Velero, as the kopia password of every backup repository — [Repository password](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/velero/#repository-password>); changing it orphans every volume backup |
| `dependency-track/sbom-upload` | `api-key` | The SBOM upload job, [Dependency-Track](<https://homelab-apps.wlkr.ch/dependency-track/#secrets>); written even when empty, so the job fails on its own rather than stalling the sync |

The two `route53` leaves are separate IAM users on purpose: cert-manager only ever writes `_acme-challenge` TXT records, though its [policy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/#configuration>) still allows any record change, while external-dns creates and deletes A records by design, so stolen it can repoint hostnames. One shared key collapses both into "someone owns your domain".

### Generated secrets

Every random value — session keys, break-glass admin passwords, OIDC client pairs — comes from an ESO `Password` generator, written into OpenBao by a `PushSecret` in the same file as the `ExternalSecret` that reads it back: `payload/platform/authentik/secrets.yaml` here, `<app>/secrets.yaml` in the workloads repository. A fresh cluster needs no prompt for them, and a workload that adds a path needs no change to this repository.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `updatePolicy: IfNotExists` | ESO checks each property before writing it and skips one that exists, so a value is written once and the next reconcile's freshly generated one is discarded |
| `deletionPolicy: None` | Deleting the `PushSecret`, or its Application, leaves the value in OpenBao; the policy grants no `delete` either |
| `symbols: 0`, `allowRepeat: true` | Alphanumeric only, so a value survives a URL, a `.env` line and a shell unquoted; repeats allowed because without them the generator cannot produce more than ten digits |
| `encoding` or a `template` where the reader wants a format | Umami's keys are hex, Dependency-Track's KEK is base64 of 32 bytes |
| One `Password` per path, its `secretKeys` the property names | A generator produces one map per call; one key per property keeps every value independent |
| Sync wave `-2` in the workloads repository | Its `ExternalSecret`s sit at `-1`, and ArgoCD waits for a wave to be healthy before the next |

ESO refuses to write into a path it did not create (`secret not managed by external-secrets`), which keeps it away from everything `make bao-secrets` wrote. Reading a generated value, such as the `akadmin` password:

```bash
kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao kv get -mount=kv -field=bootstrap-password authentik/config
```

### Operator credential

No root token outlives the command that needs it. `make bao-init` ends by creating a userpass login for the scripts and revoking the root token; the password lands in `output/credentials/openbao-operator.json` (mode `0600`). The policy and login are written by `bao_create_operator` in `scripts/lib/bao.sh`.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| The `operator` policy: `kv/` read, write and delete, `sys/storage/raft/snapshot` read | Everything `make bao-secrets`, `make claude-session-pat`, [rotation](<#rotating-a-credential>) and a [snapshot](<#backups>) need; policies, auth methods and snapshot restores still need root |
| `sys/generate-root-token/*` and `sys/decode-token` in the same policy | Since OpenBao 2.6 `bao operator generate-root` needs a token, so without these a revoked root could not be regenerated; the unseal shares still decide |
| `token_ttl` and `token_max_ttl`, short | The scripts cache the token in the pod; one a dropped connection leaves behind expires on its own, and the exit trap revokes it sooner |
| Userpass, not OIDC | Authentik reads its own database password from OpenBao, so an Authentik login would be a loop |
| The scripts fall back to the root token in `openbao-init.json` | A cluster initialised before this keeps working, with a warning, until `make bao-rotate-root` creates the login and revokes the root token |

### Kubernetes auth

ESO authenticates with a short-lived ServiceAccount JWT, which OpenBao validates against the TokenReview API (`rbac.yaml` binds `system:auth-delegator` to the `openbao` ServiceAccount) and answers with a token bound to one policy. Three `ClusterSecretStore`s in `cluster-secret-store.yaml` each log in with their own role, so what a namespace can reach follows from the store it is allowed to use:

| Store | Who may use it | Logs in as | Reaches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `openbao` | The platform namespaces | `external-secrets-vault` in `external-secrets` | Reads every path, because Authentik reads each workload's `kv/<app>/config`; writes only `authentik/`, `monitoring/` and `velero/`, where its `PushSecret`s are |
| `openbao-apps` | Every other namespace | `external-secrets-vault` in the `ExternalSecret`'s own namespace | `kv/<namespace>/` |
| `openbao-claude-agents` | `claude-agents` | The same, in `claude-agents` | `kv/claude-*`, where `make claude-session-pat` writes each session's token |

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `openbao-apps` names no ServiceAccount namespace | ESO then requests the token in the namespace of the `ExternalSecret` or `PushSecret`, and the `external-secrets-apps` policy templates that namespace, as OpenBao read it from the token, into its paths. One role serves every workload, and a new one needs no change here |
| `openbao` lists the platform namespaces by name, `openbao-apps` excludes the same list | Their prefixes hold the platform's credentials; a label would not do, because a workload may ship its own `Namespace` with any label. A platform component that reads a secret from a new namespace adds it to both |
| Each workload ships an `external-secrets-vault` ServiceAccount | The role is bound to that name; `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, because only ESO needs a token for it |
| Referent stores report `Valid` without logging in | ESO cannot know the namespace until an `ExternalSecret` names the store, so a missing role or ServiceAccount shows on the `ExternalSecret`, not the store |

The ServiceAccount the platform store uses lives in `cluster-secret-store.yaml` too, because the stores only validate against a running, unsealed OpenBao. `make bao-init` writes the policies and roles on a fresh cluster by running `scripts/bao-policies.sh`; after a change to that script, `make bao-policies` rewrites them on a live one. It needs a root token, because the operator login cannot write policies: run it before `make bao-rotate-root`, or with a [generated root token](<#generating-a-root-token>).

## Usage

### Bootstrap

1. Initialise, unseal and configure the engine and ESO's auth. Safe to re-run: each configuration step is skipped if already in place, and an initialised cluster is left alone.

   ```bash
   make bao-init
   ```

   > **Move the unseal keys before you do anything else**
   >
   > `make bao-init` writes the unseal keys to `output/credentials/openbao-init.json` and the [operator login](<#operator-credential>) to `openbao-operator.json` beside it (mode `0600`, gitignored) — a plaintext copy of the keys to every secret the cluster holds, next to the [etcd encryption key](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md>). The root token in the first file is revoked before the command ends. Copy both into a password manager that does not need this cluster to be running, then delete the key file. Losing the keys means the data is unrecoverable: no support line, no recovery flow.
2. Write the values that belong to outside accounts — the prompts follow [Quickstart step 11](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md>). The generated paths need nothing: their `PushSecret`s write them once the store validates.

   ```bash
   make bao-secrets
   ```
3. Confirm the stores validate:

   ```bash
   kubectl get clustersecretstore
   ```

### Authenticating locally

```bash
kubectl -n openbao port-forward svc/openbao-active 8200:8200 &   # a standby rejects requests
export BAO_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200
bao login -method=userpass username=operator   # password from openbao-operator.json
```

### Storing and reading a secret

```bash
bao kv put kv/cert-manager/route53 access-key-id='AKIA...' secret-access-key='...'
printf '%s' '{"access-key-id":"AKIA...","secret-access-key":"..."}' \
  | bao kv put -mount=kv cert-manager/route53 -     # what make bao-secrets does: JSON on stdin
bao kv get kv/cert-manager/route53
```

### Rotating a credential

A typed value is rotated with `make bao-secrets`, which asks per existing path whether to overwrite it; a generated one by deleting its path, after which the `PushSecret` writes a whole new set within its `refreshInterval`.

1. Rotate the path. For a typed value, answer `y` for that path; the others are left alone. `FORCE=1 make bao-secrets` overwrites every ordinary path without asking; `kneadtime/config` still wants a typed `OVERWRITE`, and without a terminal every existing path is left alone.

   ```bash
   make bao-secrets
   ```

   For a generated path, delete it. Every key in it changes, with the consequences the reading component's page lists — for `authentik/config` that is every session, token and platform OIDC client at once:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao kv metadata delete -mount=kv <path>
   ```
2. Push the new value into the `Secret` now rather than at the next `refreshInterval` — see [External Secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/#usage>):

   ```bash
   kubectl annotate externalsecret -n <namespace> <name> force-sync=$(date +%s) --overwrite
   ```
3. Restart whatever read the old value into an environment variable; a rotated `Secret` reaches a running pod only through a rollout.

## Health check

```bash
for pod in $(kubectl -n openbao get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=openbao -o name); do
  kubectl -n openbao exec "$pod" -- bao status
done
kubectl get clustersecretstore
kubectl get externalsecret -A
```

`bao status` should show `Initialized: true`, `Sealed: false`, and `HA Mode: active` on one pod with `standby` on the others; it exits `0` unsealed, `2` sealed and `1` unreachable. Every `ClusterSecretStore` should report `Ready=True`.

`prometheusrule.yaml` mails `OpenBaoSealed` for each pod sealed past the rule's `for`, read from the `openbao-sealed` pod label because a sealed pod still reports Ready, and `OpenBaoNoActiveNode` when no unsealed active pod is scraped at all.

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Sealed after every restart, and Ready does not mean unsealed**
>
> OpenBao seals itself on every pod restart — node reboot, chart bump, Kured — and no auto-unseal is configured, so it stays shut until someone with the key shares unseals it. The readiness and liveness probes answer healthy while sealed (`sealedcode=204`), deliberately, so a StatefulSet rollout does not stop at the first pod waiting for keys and a sealed pod is not restarted into another sealed pod; the cost is that only `bao status`, not `kubectl get pods`, can tell you OpenBao is usable. While sealed no `ExternalSecret` resolves, so cert-manager loses its Route53 credentials and nothing breaks until a certificate expires up to sixty days later, with no obvious link to the reboot. See [Limitations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/limitations/index.md>).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A `PushSecret` cannot add a key to a path `make bao-secrets` wrote**
>
> Paths written before their `PushSecret` existed carry no `managed-by` metadata, so a new key on one fails with `secret not managed by external-secrets` and the `PushSecret` goes Degraded. The existing keys are unaffected. Mark the path as ESO's once, and the next reconcile adds the key: `bao kv metadata put -mount=kv -custom-metadata=managed-by=external-secrets <path>`.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **`#` and `!` on a command line**
>
> Inside double quotes an interactive bash expands `!` from history before the quotes are considered, and an unquoted `#` truncates the line. Both are silent and store a plausible credential that does not work. Use single quotes, or write the secret as JSON and pass `@file` — a missing file then fails loudly.

## Recovery

### Unsealing after a restart

```bash
make bao-unseal
```

It feeds a threshold of shares from `output/credentials/openbao-init.json` to each sealed replica, waits for one that has not joined Raft yet, and is idempotent. With the key file deleted, which is the correct end state, unseal by hand:

```bash
for pod in $(kubectl -n openbao get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=openbao -o name); do
  kubectl -n openbao exec "$pod" -- bao status >/dev/null 2>&1
  case $? in
    0) echo "$pod: already unsealed" ;;
    2) for i in 1 2 3; do
         kubectl -n openbao exec -it "$pod" -- bao operator unseal
       done ;;
    *) echo "$pod: OpenBao did not answer, check the pod" ;;
  esac
done
```

A replica that says `Vault is not initialized` has not joined the Raft cluster — one that predates the `retry_join` stanzas or started before `openbao-0` was initialised. Point it at the leader once; it takes unseal keys afterwards:

```bash
kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-1 -- \
  bao operator raft join http://openbao-0.openbao-internal:8200
```

### Generating a root token

For what the operator policy does not cover — a policy, an auth method, a snapshot restore, or the operator login itself broken. Needs the operator login and a threshold of unseal shares; each step runs in the pod.

1. Log in as the operator; it prompts for the password from `openbao-operator.json`.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec -it openbao-0 -- bao login -method=userpass username=operator
   ```
2. Generate a one-time password and start the attempt with it; note both the OTP and the nonce.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao operator generate-root -generate-otp
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao operator generate-root -init -otp=<otp>
   ```
3. Enter one share per run until the threshold is met; the last prints `Encoded Token`.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec -it openbao-0 -- bao operator generate-root -nonce=<nonce>
   ```
4. Decode it into the root token.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao operator generate-root -decode=<encoded-token> -otp=<otp>
   ```
5. Do the one job with it, then revoke it and clear the pod's token cache.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec -i openbao-0 -- bao login -     # paste the root token, then Ctrl-D
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao token revoke -self
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- sh -c 'rm -f "$HOME/.bao-token"'
   ```

With the operator login gone too, no token can start an attempt: set `disable_unauthed_generate_root_endpoints = false` in the listener stanza in `application.yaml`, restart and unseal the pods, and drive the deprecated `sys/generate-root/*` API with the shares; revert the setting afterwards.

To recreate the operator login with that root token, put it as `root_token` into a copy of `openbao-init.json`, move `openbao-operator.json` aside, and run `make bao-rotate-root`, which writes a new password and revokes the token.

### Backups

Logged in as the operator through the `openbao-active` port-forward from [Authenticating locally](<#authenticating-locally>); its policy covers the snapshot, and a standby refuses it:

```bash
bao operator raft snapshot save snapshot.bao
```

The snapshot holds all KV data and OpenBao's own configuration; restore with `bao operator raft snapshot restore`. Store it off-cluster — it is encrypted with a key that exists only in the unseal shares, so it is exactly as recoverable as your key custody. See [Backups &amp; Recovery](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md>).

# Rook-Ceph

Distributed block storage using [Rook](<https://rook.io/>) as the Kubernetes operator for [Ceph](<https://ceph.io/>). It is the component that still has your data after a node dies, and the one with the steepest learning curve. Check `ceph status` more often than seems necessary and never ignore a `WARN`.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `rook-ceph` |
| Depends on | A raw `rook-osd` partition on every worker, written at install time |
| If it is down | Every pod with a volume — `openbao` first, which turns a storage problem into a cluster problem |
| Health check | `make storage-check` — it binds a real PVC, which `ceph status` alone does not prove |
| UI | `rook.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` |
| Files | `payload/platform/rook-ceph-operator/`: the `rook-ceph` chart, the operator itself. `payload/platform/rook-ceph-cluster/`: the `rook-ceph-cluster` chart, whose `valuesObject` holds the `CephCluster`, the object store and the storage classes. `payload/platform/rook-ceph/`: the CSI driver and its RBAC, the dashboards and the UI route |

## Configuration

### Disks

Each worker has a raw partition labelled `rook-osd`, created by Ignition as the **last** partition with whatever the root leaves, which Rook adds as an OSD; data is replicated three ways across them. Control planes get none, and the CephCluster's OSD placement excludes them: on one shared NVMe, etcd's fsyncs and BlueStore's writes stalled each other until OSDs hit their heartbeat timeout and aborted. Its contents are wherever Ceph last wrote them, so inserting a partition ahead of it shifts its offset and takes the OSD data with it: changing the partition table is a [reinstall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md>), not an edit.

Ignition declares it with `format: none` and `wipe_filesystem: true`, because `ceph-volume` reads the BlueStore *signature*, not the partition table, and a reinstalled node that kept the old bytes would present an OSD from a cluster that no longer exists. Ceph declines any device that already carries a filesystem — the first thing to check when an OSD refuses to appear, see [No OSDs after reprovisioning](<#no-osds-after-reprovisioning>).

### Storage classes

| StorageClass | Provides | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rook-ceph-block` | RBD block volumes, cluster default | `ReadWriteOnce` only; `ReadWriteMany` needs CephFS, which is not enabled. Block PVs are deleted with their claim, and every Application prunes, so removing a PVC from Git removes the volume — see [Backups](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md>) |
| `ceph-bucket` | S3 buckets from the object store | Reclaim `Retain`, so deleting a claim cannot delete the bucket |

### Object storage

A `CephObjectStore` provides an S3 endpoint at `http://rook-ceph-rgw-object-store.rook-ceph.svc`, so backups and log chunks live somewhere other than the block pool they protect. The infra Gateway publishes the same endpoint as `https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` for [Velero](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/velero/#configuration>), whose S3 client only signs cleanly over TLS. More than one RGW instance (`gateway.instances`) keeps a node reboot from stalling a backup, which only holds while they sit on separate nodes: `gateway.placement` carries the spread constraint, because the `placement.all` block belongs to the `CephCluster` and never reaches this CR. It is a hard one: every gateway is daemon `a`, so on one node the exporter reports their counters under the same labels and Prometheus drops them, and the descheduler never evicts a `system-cluster-critical` pod to fix that. The data pool is erasure coded (`dataChunks` and `codingChunks`): less overhead than three replicas, safe at `failureDomain: host` only with more workers than chunks.

### Monitoring

In `rook-ceph-cluster/application.yaml`'s `valuesObject`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `cephClusterSpec.monitoring.enabled` | Turns on the mgr `prometheus` module and lets the operator maintain a `ServiceMonitor`. Without it a degraded pool, a down OSD or a near-full cluster is invisible to Prometheus, and a full Ceph cluster stops accepting writes |
| `monitoring.createPrometheusRules` | Ships Ceph's own alerting rules as a `PrometheusRule`. Its CRD comes from the `prometheus-operator-crds` Application; a sync before it lands fails and is retried — see [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/#crds>) |
| `cephClusterSpec.cephConfig` `mgr/dashboard/*` | Sets the dashboard's Prometheus and Grafana links through the mon config store, which the operator reapplies on every reconcile, rather than a one-off `ceph dashboard set-*` Job |
| `mon_cluster_log_level: info` | The Ceph default is `debug`, and the mons copy the cluster log to stderr, so Rook's probes and the mgr's pgmap ticks became most of the mon log volume in [Loki](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>). Warnings and errors are unaffected |

Rook's Grafana dashboards are vendored in `grafana-dashboards.yaml` — see [Monitoring → Dashboards](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/#dashboards>).

### CSI driver

From Rook v1.20 the RBD driver is deployed by the ceph-csi-operator subchart, which deploys nothing until an `OperatorConfig` and a `Driver` CR tell it what to run. Neither chart ships them, so they live in `csi-driver.yaml`; without them every PVC stays `Pending` on `ExternalProvisioning`.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `csi-driver.yaml` in `rook-ceph`, with `SkipDryRunOnMissingResource` | The CRs need the ceph-csi-operator's CRDs, which arrive with the operator chart |
| `OperatorConfig` pointing at the chart's image-set `ConfigMap` | A chart bump moves every sidecar and the cephcsi image together |
| Driver name `rook-ceph.rbd.csi.ceph.com` | Derived from the namespace and must match the StorageClasses' `provisioner`. RBD is the only driver; CephFS is not enabled |
| Two controller plugin replicas, `RollingUpdate` without surge, a PodDisruptionBudget | A drain of the provisioner's node otherwise stalls every provision, attach, resize and snapshot until the pod reschedules. The operator already keeps the replicas on distinct nodes with required anti-affinity and runs every sidecar with leader election, so the `Driver` CR carries no spread constraint, and no field for one |
| `csi-rbac.yaml` | The ceph-csi-operator creates no ServiceAccounts, and the names are fixed by `CSI_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_PREFIX` (empty here): `rbd-ctrlplugin-sa` and `rbd-nodeplugin-sa`. Without them the Deployment and DaemonSet exist but create no pods |

> [!WARNING]
>
> **`csi` values on the operator chart do nothing**
>
> Helm accepts values a chart no longer reads. Driver settings go in `csi-driver.yaml`.

`csi-rbac.yaml` is the RBD half of the ceph-csi-operator's `deploy/multifile/csi-rbac.yaml` at the version the rook-ceph chart pulls in; Renovate does not see it. To refresh it:

1. Fetch and rename:

   ```bash
   curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ceph/ceph-csi-operator/vX.Y.Z/deploy/multifile/csi-rbac.yaml \
     | sed -e 's/ceph-csi-operator-system/rook-ceph/' -e 's/ceph-csi-operator-//'
   ```
2. Keep only the rbd documents (CephFS, NFS and NVMe-oF are not enabled).
3. Re-indent the sequences for yamllint and prefix the cluster-scoped names.
4. Cut the nodeplugin ClusterRole back: drop `secrets`, `serviceaccounts` and `serviceaccounts/token`, and keep `get` on the `rook-csi-rbd-node` and `rook-csi-rbd-provisioner` Secrets in the `rbd-nodeplugin-r` Role. Its token sits on every node; upstream's grants serve only the encryption KMS providers, which nothing here uses, and minting any ServiceAccount's token is cluster-admin.

### cephx keys stay on aes

Ceph 20 warns about the legacy `aes` cipher, and every key here is deliberately on it: the kernel client krbd does not implement `aes256k`, so CSI keys moved to it make every `rbd map` fail with `map failed: (22) Invalid argument` while Ceph reports the rotation a success. Two ciphers in one cluster trigger `AUTH_EMERGENCY_CIPHERS_SET` and buy no security. In `rook-ceph-cluster/application.yaml`'s `valuesObject`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `keyType: aes` | krbd cannot use anything else |
| `mon_auth_allow_insecure_key: "true"` | Its default differs between mons; one that says `false` refuses an OSD's start-up key fetch, and an OSD whose on-disk key predates a rotation then fails with `Permission denied` |
| `keyRotationPolicy: KeyGeneration` | Changing `keyType` alone never rotates existing keys while the policy is `Disabled` |
| `keyGeneration` | Rotation only triggers on an increase, so a generation can never be lowered to undo one |
| `healthCheck.muteHealthWarning` | The `AUTH_*` warnings would otherwise keep the Application `Degraded` while the data is healthy. Temporary: remove once RBD moves to the userspace `rbd-nbd` mounter and the keys can leave `aes` |

## Usage

### Requesting a volume

Any workload can claim the default class:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: my-app-data
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
```

Add `storageClassName: rook-ceph-block` to say so explicitly. A Deployment with two replicas sharing one RWO PVC schedules one pod and leaves the other in `ContainerCreating` with a multi-attach error.

### Requesting a bucket

Ask for an `ObjectBucketClaim`; Rook creates the bucket and writes a `ConfigMap` (`BUCKET_NAME`, `BUCKET_HOST`, `BUCKET_PORT`) and a `Secret` (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`) sharing the claim's name:

```yaml
apiVersion: objectbucket.io/v1alpha1
kind: ObjectBucketClaim
metadata:
  name: my-app-bucket
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  generateBucketName: my-app
  storageClassName: ceph-bucket
```

## Health check

### Is storage ready?

```bash
make storage-check
```

Run it after the GitOps handover, before trusting anything that mounts a volume: a `CephCluster` reports `Ready` with no OSDs, and a `StorageClass` exists whether or not a CSI driver registered for it. The script walks the chain in the order it breaks and stops at the first missing link:

| Check | What its absence means |
| --- | --- |
| `CephCluster` is `Ready` | the cluster Application has not synced yet |
| an OSD pod is `Running` | Rook took no disk — see [No OSDs after reprovisioning](<#no-osds-after-reprovisioning>) |
| `ceph health` is not `HEALTH_ERR` | Ceph itself is unwell; `HEALTH_WARN` is allowed through |
| the CSI driver is registered | no `Driver` CR, so the ceph-csi-operator deployed nothing |
| node plugin and provisioner are up | usually a ServiceAccount the DaemonSet cannot find |
| a 1 GiB PVC binds and is cleaned up | the only check that proves the other five |

The last one asks for a volume the way a workload would and waits `TIMEOUT` seconds (default in `scripts/storage-check.sh`); `NAMESPACE` and `CLASS` override where and what it asks for.

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Ceph warnings show as Degraded**
>
> ArgoCD maps `HEALTH_WARN` to Degraded, so `rook-ceph-cluster` reports Degraded for the whole of a warning; nothing else waits on it — see [GitOps](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md>).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Rook skips tainted nodes**
>
> The operator neither creates nor updates an OSD on a node with a taint `placement.all` does not tolerate, `PreferNoSchedule` included, and logs `placement settings do not match`. [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) taints every node waiting for its reboot lock, so that taint is tolerated.

## Recovery

### No OSDs after reprovisioning

A node whose `rook-osd` partition still carries a previous cluster's BlueStore signature gets no OSD: the `CephCluster` reports `Ready` with `HEALTH_WARN`, `kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods -l app=rook-ceph-osd` is empty, and the first PVC — `data-openbao-0` on a fresh bootstrap — stays `Pending`.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **The old cluster's data is already gone**
>
> Once the mons that held the cluster map left with the old control plane, those OSDs cannot be re-adopted by anything. Take a backup off the disks *before* a rebuild if you need one.

1. Confirm the cause:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n rook-ceph logs job/rook-ceph-osd-prepare-<node> | tail -3
   # skipping device "nvme0n1p10" because it contains a filesystem "ceph_bluestore"
   # skipping osd.3: "..." belonging to a different ceph cluster "..."
   ```
2. Rebuild the node, steps 3 to 7 of [Rebuilding or repartitioning a node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/#rebuilding-or-repartitioning-a-node>): `make reinstall` only arms the PXE menu, and the [installer](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md>) wipes the disk when the node network-boots.
3. If the node cannot be rebuilt now, wipe the partition by hand over SSH. `wipefs` removes the signature Rook skips on; the `dd` removes the BlueStore label behind it. Address it by label, as Ignition does, rather than by the device name in the log:

   ```bash
   sudo wipefs -a /dev/disk/by-partlabel/rook-osd
   sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/disk/by-partlabel/rook-osd bs=1M count=200
   ```
4. Restart the operator so it recreates the `osd-prepare` jobs:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n rook-ceph rollout restart deploy/rook-ceph-operator
   ```
5. Confirm an OSD per node and a binding PVC:

   ```bash
   make storage-check
   ```

# Security Policies

Five cluster-wide controls: Pod Security Admission, default-deny network policy in both directions, a host firewall on the nodes, no API token on the `default` ServiceAccount, and admission policies on image references, namespace labels and the `authentik` namespace. Each is easy to turn on and hard to turn on safely, so the pattern is the same for all of them: measure first, enforce second, one namespace at a time.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system` for the Application; it owns Namespace objects across the cluster |
| Depends on | [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md>) to enforce the network policies |
| If it is down | Nothing at the time; the labels and policies stay applied and only stop being corrected |
| Health check | `kubectl get ns -L pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce`, `kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicy` |
| Pruning | Enabled, except for the Namespaces: each carries `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false`, because pruning a Namespace deletes everything inside it, PVCs included. Anything else removed from Git is pruned, so the Application does not sit OutOfSync on leftovers |
| Files | `payload/platform/security/`, the network policies one file per namespace under `network-policies/`, plus the CoreDNS PodDisruptionBudget — see [Components](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/#components>) |

## Configuration

### Pod Security Admission

A namespace without labels gets the cluster default from `ansible/templates/admission.yaml.j2`: `enforce` at `baseline`, `audit` and `warn` at `restricted`. It reaches a control-plane node only at provisioning; see [Node hardening](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/#node-hardening>). It exempts `kube-system`, which Cilium needs before Argo CD can label anything, and the namespaces that need `privileged` but carry no labels. An exemption skips `audit` and `warn` as well, so the labelled namespaces below are not exempt. Each namespace in `pod-security.yaml` carries three labels:

| Label | Set to | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enforce` | The level the namespace demonstrably needs | Rejects pods that violate it |
| `audit` | Stricter | Records violations in the [API server audit log](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>) |
| `warn` | Stricter | Warns whoever applies the manifest |

Enforcement is set to what already works, so nothing running breaks, while `warn` and `audit` show what a stricter level would catch; tightening later is an informed change.

The level per namespace is in `pod-security.yaml`; the rule behind it:

| Enforce | Which namespaces | Why not stricter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `privileged` | Those with a component on the host: the CNI and control plane, Ceph's OSDs, node-exporter, Trivy's node-collector, the etcd jobs and Velero's node-agent, Alloy, Kured | Host networking, the host PID namespace, raw block devices or a hostPath under the kubelet, etcd or log directories, all of which `baseline` forbids. node-exporter has a namespace of its own (`namespaceOverride`) so the rest of the monitoring stack need not follow it |
| `baseline` | Those with a container that starts as root or escalates: Grafana's `init-chown-data`, the runners and their job pods, and the operators not yet checked against `restricted` | Reduced when the chart offers a non-root path, one namespace at a time |
| `restricted` | Everything else, and the namespaces that run no pods | — |

`privileged` here means "not yet reduced", not "unexamined": `audit` and `warn` are still `baseline` or `restricted` on all of them. Namespace objects are owned by this Application so the labels stay declarative rather than drifting after `CreateNamespace=true`. `cilium-secrets` is the exception: the Cilium chart creates it, so its labels are `secretsNamespaceLabels` in `payload/platform/cilium/values.yaml`, and a second owner would fight the first. Workload namespaces label themselves in the workloads repository, and `namespace-privileged-allowed` keeps them off `privileged`.

### Network policies

One file per namespace in `network-policies/`, holding that namespace's `CiliumNetworkPolicy` objects. A namespace gets two whole-namespace policies, `default-ingress` and `default-egress`, so every pod in it is default-deny in both directions, plus one policy per workload that needs more than the rest of the namespace does. Each policy's `description` is the record of who may connect and why; the rules are not repeated here. `cluster-wide.yaml` holds the `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` objects: the rules every pod gets, so a namespace file is the record of what its namespace may do *beyond* those.

#### Why CiliumNetworkPolicy and not NetworkPolicy

Two kinds of traffic have no pod identity a standard `NetworkPolicy` can name: Gateway traffic, which reaches a backend from the per-node Envoy, and kubelet health probes, which come from the node. A plain default-deny therefore kills ingress *and* probes, and the pods restart forever in a way that looks like an application fault. Cilium's `fromEntities` names them: `ingress` for Envoy-proxied traffic, `host` and `remote-node` for the kubelet.

#### Cluster-wide rules

A rule that is word-for-word the same in every namespace file is lifted into `cluster-wide.yaml`, selecting every endpoint that has a namespace and with `enableDefaultDeny` off in both directions. The selector is not `{}` because that also takes the Gateway's `reserved:ingress` endpoint and the health endpoint, which then carry a policy they have no use for. Default deny is off because a cluster-wide egress rule would otherwise put every pod in a namespace without policies into egress default-deny. DNS is the only rule lifted; the intra-namespace and node-probe rules would qualify but change what a namespace file says, so they stay.

The second policy there, `init`, is for the seconds before the agent has resolved a new pod's labels. The pod then carries the reserved `init` identity, which no namespace policy selects, and the audit log shows its traffic denied all the same; a scan Job's first lookups and a starting pod's probes were the bulk of the audit log. It admits the node, DNS out and DNS in, nothing else.

The third, `cnpg-backups`, selects every CloudNativePG pod by its `cnpg.io/cluster` label and admits only the object store, by the same two rules Velero's namespace has. Every database's backup sidecar needs exactly that, wherever the database runs, so one policy replaces a rule in each workload's file.

#### What every policy contains

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Ingress from within the namespace | Replicas, sidecars and a workload's own database talk to each other on ports that change with the chart |
| Ingress from `host` and `remote-node` | Kubelet probes come from the node, and so do the API server's webhook calls, the aggregation layer and `kubectl port-forward`; all of them carry the node's identity, on a control-plane node with the `kube-apiserver` label as well |
| Ingress from `ingress` | Only where an HTTPRoute sends the Gateway's Envoy straight at the namespace; a namespace behind the Authentik outpost admits `authentik` instead. Kept at L4: the HTTPRoute is already the L7 filter for that traffic |
| Ingress from `monitoring` on the scraped port, `GET /metrics` | The one port a ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor names, at L7, so the scraper can open nothing else |
| Egress within the namespace, and to `kube-apiserver` where there is a Kubernetes client | The `kube-apiserver` entity is the endpoints behind `kubernetes.default`; no pod uses the kube-vip address. DNS is not repeated: the cluster-wide rule above sends every lookup through the proxy, which is what makes `toFQDNs` work and every lookup visible in Hubble |
| Egress to external names as `toFQDNs` | A name reads as the dependency it is; an address does not. The Gateway's own addresses count as external: a pod calling `auth.k8s.wlkr.ch` is classified `world`, not `ingress` |
| Egress to the backend pod as well, when the name is one the Gateway serves | The Gateway's Envoy checks the caller's egress policy a second time, against the backend pod it picked and that pod's port, and answers `403 Access denied` itself when no rule matches; audit mode never sees it. The OIDC clients of Authentik carry both rules |
| HTTP rules on plaintext ports, ingress side only | A request crossing a namespace boundary is proxied once, by the receiving node. TLS and gRPC ports stay at L4; the proxy cannot read them. A machine caller gets the methods and paths a week of Hubble records showed; a browser UI behind the Authentik outpost stays at `http: [{}]`, its paths being the application's own. The path is matched with its query string: a rule anchored with `$` names the query as well, as OpenBao's `/v1/sys/metrics\?format=prometheus$` does |

Host-networked pods (Cilium, kube-vip, the control plane, node-exporter, Tetragon, the CSI node plugins) have no endpoint of their own and cannot be selected; to everything else they are `host` or `remote-node`. `kube-system` therefore covers only its pod-networked workloads, each selected by label.

Where a chart ships `NetworkPolicy` objects of its own (`argocd`) they are switched off in its values: Cilium unions the two kinds, so a chart rule that allows everything would silently override the default-deny.

### Host firewall

Pod policies cannot select a host-networked port. A `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` with a `nodeSelector` can, and Cilium's [host firewall](<https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/host-firewall/>) enforces it on the native device and `cilium_host`. What each port is for is in [Host Firewall Inventory 2026-10-30](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/host-firewall-inventory-2026-10-30/index.md>).

| Behaviour | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Only packets addressed to a node IP are checked | The kube-vip address counts on the node holding it; Gateway addresses and NodePorts are translated first, so their policy is the backend pod's |
| A node with no selecting policy is not denied anything on IPv4 | The switch can merge alone, and reverting the policy needs no second rollout |
| No rule in a direction leaves that direction unenforced | A host policy with `ingress` only never blocks a node's own connections, and their replies pass through conntrack |
| Host endpoint labels are filtered | `kubernetes.io/hostname` is not among them, so a node can only be chosen by a label such as `node-access` in the upstream example, or by the `control-plane` role label |
| A pod reaching another node's IP is masqueraded to its own node | The target sees `remote-node`, so the firewall can tell the LAN from the cluster but not Prometheus from any other pod; the source pod's egress policy decides that |

`network-policies/host-firewall.yaml` selects the nodes carrying `host-firewall.wlkr.ch/selected`. It denies the LAN everything but SSH, the API server, DHCP and ping, and admits the whole cluster to every port, since a narrower cluster rule could not name Prometheus and could lock out a node.

### Default ServiceAccount tokens

A pod that names no `serviceAccountName` lands on `default`, which nothing configures, and gets an API token it has no use for. A workload reaching the API through `default` is already a misconfiguration, so `default-serviceaccounts.yaml` sets `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on it in every namespace with nothing to preserve, empty namespaces included. Left out: `kube-system`, where the control plane authenticates with client certificates and "very likely fine" is not the standard. `authentik-server` runs on `default` by chart default and is covered: Authentik's Kubernetes calls are worker tasks, which run under the `authentik` account.

The same rule applies to a chart workload whose own ServiceAccount has no binding — Alertmanager, Cilium's Envoy and Argo CD's HAProxy switch the mount off in their values — unless the process needs the in-cluster config to start at all ([the External Secrets webhook](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/#configuration>)) or the chart offers no switch (Rook's `rook-ceph-default` and `rook-ceph-rgw`).

### Agent RBAC

`claude-agent-rbac.yaml` gives the in-cluster Claude Code agents two ClusterRoles for the `claude-reader` and `claude-writer` ServiceAccounts of the `claude-agents` namespace. Cluster-scoped RBAC cannot come from the `apps` project, and what an agent may touch is a platform decision.

| Role | Bound | Grants | Leaves out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude-agent-read` | Cluster-wide, to both ServiceAccounts | `get`, `list`, `watch` on named core, workload and CRD kinds, `pods/log` included | Secrets, RBAC, webhooks, CRDs, `pods/exec`, Trivy's exposed-secret reports |
| `claude-agent-write` | Nowhere by the platform: the workloads repository adds a RoleBinding in each namespace a writer session may change | Create, update, patch and delete on pods, workloads, Services, ConfigMaps, jobs, autoscalers and disruption budgets | The above, plus PersistentVolumeClaims (deleting one deletes data), NetworkPolicies and routes (they change who may reach what, which is a pull request) |

- **Creating a pod reads every Secret in its namespace.** That is why the write role is bound per namespace, and the `apps` project cannot place a RoleBinding in the namespaces its [destinations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/#projects>) exclude.
- **`claude-writer-pod-limits`** in `admission-policies.yaml` refuses any pod or pod template from the writer that uses the host's network, PID or IPC namespace, a `hostPath` volume, a privileged container, or a ServiceAccount other than `default` or the one the workload already runs as. A namespace without a Pod Security level allows all of those, and another ServiceAccount's token is that account's RBAC.
- **`pods/log` is cluster-wide**, so the reader sees whatever any component logs, platform namespaces included. Triage needs it, and a cluster-wide grant cannot leave out namespaces.

Kinds are listed, never wildcarded, so a new CRD is invisible to the agents until someone adds it. Argo CD reverts a hand edit within minutes either way.

### Admission policies

Trivy reports a bad image after it is running; `admission-policies.yaml` refuses or records it at admission, with the built-in `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` rather than a policy engine. The image policies match Pods and every controller that produces them, so a bad Deployment is rejected at `kubectl apply` rather than failing quietly in its ReplicaSet. The other three close what RBAC and the `apps` project cannot express.

| Policy | Action | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `image-tag-pinned` | `Deny` | A tag other than `latest`, or a digest. Nothing running violates it, and an unpinned image is the one Renovate can neither track nor roll back |
| `image-registry-allowed` | `Audit` and `Warn` | The registries the cluster pulls from today; a reference with no registry counts as `docker.io`. Recorded to the [audit log](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>) and shown to whoever applies, not enforced, until the record is clean |
| `claude-writer-pod-limits` | `Deny` | Host access and borrowed ServiceAccounts from the agent writer, see [Agent RBAC](<#agent-rbac>) |
| `namespace-privileged-allowed` | `Deny` | A Namespace may carry `enforce: privileged` only if it is in the policy's list, the `privileged` rows above. The `apps` project creates its own Namespaces and their labels, so without it a workload could opt out of Pod Security |
| `authentik-foreign-objects` | `Deny` | In `authentik`, an object an Argo CD Application applied must come from `authentik` or `security`, or be the ConfigMap `authentik-blueprint-<application>`. Argo CD cannot whitelist kinds per destination namespace, so this is what holds `apps` to its blueprint there; objects with no `argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id` annotation, from controllers and `kubectl`, are not matched |

All but one carry `failurePolicy: Ignore`: an expression that errors lets the request through rather than stopping every pod in the cluster. A real violation is still refused. `claude-writer-pod-limits` fails closed, since it only ever matches one identity.

## Usage

### Promoting the registry allowlist

1. Confirm nothing running would be refused, over the full Loki retention:

   ```text
   {job="kubernetes-audit"} |= "validation.policy.admission.k8s.io/validation_failure" |= "image-registry-allowed"
   ```
2. Change `validationActions` on the binding in `admission-policies.yaml` to `["Deny"]`.

### Tightening a namespace

1. See what running pods a stricter level would reject, without changing anything:

   ```bash
   kubectl label --dry-run=server --overwrite ns cert-manager \
     pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
   ```
2. Catch what is not running right now — a nightly CronJob, say — from the `audit` label's records over the full Loki retention window, in Grafana:

   ```text
   {job="kubernetes-audit"} |= "pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-violations"
   ```
3. Raise `enforce` in `pod-security.yaml`.

### Rollout

A new policy is enforced on arrival: `policyAuditMode` in `payload/platform/cilium/values.yaml` is off. Switched on, it makes every agent evaluate each verdict and log it with `AUDIT` instead of dropping, and those verdicts reach Loki the way drops do. The mode is cluster-wide, so while it is on the older policies are not enforced either, which is why a batch of new policies goes through it together.

1. Merge the values change; the agents roll on their own. `Enabled` on every node before anything else merges:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system rollout status ds/cilium
   kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -c cilium-agent -- cilium-dbg config get PolicyAuditMode
   ```
2. Merge the policies and let them run for a week. What enforcement would have refused, by namespace pair:

   ```promql
   sum by (source_namespace, destination_namespace) (increase(hubble_policy_verdicts_total{action="audit"}[7d]))
   ```

   and flow by flow, in Grafana:

   ```text
   {job="hubble", verdict="AUDIT"} | json | line_format "{{.flow_source_namespace}}/{{.flow_source_pod_name}} -> {{.flow_destination_namespace}}/{{.flow_destination_pod_name}} {{.flow_l4_TCP_destination_port}}{{.flow_l4_UDP_destination_port}}"
   ```
3. Add a rule for every audited flow that is legitimate. Layer 7 rules are never audited: a request an HTTP rule does not match is answered `403` on the spot, which is why a new policy carries `http: [{}]` — proxied and recorded, nothing refused — until the week's requests have been read:

   ```text
   {job="hubble"} | json | flow_l7_http_method != "" | line_format "{{.flow_source_namespace}} -> {{.flow_destination_namespace}}:{{.flow_l4_TCP_destination_port}} {{.flow_l7_http_method}} {{.flow_l7_http_url}}"
   ```
4. Tighten each `http: [{}]` to the methods and paths seen, set `policyAuditMode: false`, which rolls the agents again. The first week's reading is [Network Policy Audit 2026-09-27](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/network-policy-audit-2026-09-27/index.md>), the reading before the flip [Network Policy Audit 2026-10-16](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/network-policy-audit-2026-10-16/index.md>). From then on the verdict to watch is `DROPPED`, live or from Loki — see [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/#health-check>) — and the [`HubblePolicyDrops`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/#alerting>) alert mails each refused connection.

If a single endpoint needs the same treatment later, audit mode can be set on it alone, until the agent restarts:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -c cilium-agent -- \
  cilium-dbg endpoint config <endpoint-id> PolicyAuditMode=Enabled
```

### Host firewall rollout

Audit is per host endpoint, a setting of the running agent: `policyAuditMode` would stop enforcing the pod policies, and upstream says the per-endpoint setting does not survive an agent restart, after which the node enforces. The audit week therefore runs through a node label, and every step before enforcement is reversible by removing that label.

1. Merge the switch; the agents roll, one node at a time. Every agent reports the firewall on the native device:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -c cilium-agent -- cilium-dbg status | grep 'Host firewall'
   ```
2. Reboot one worker with no policy selecting it and watch it return `Ready`, as in [Rebooting a node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/#rebooting-a-node>).
3. Merge `payload/platform/cilium/host-firewall-audit.yaml`, a DaemonSet that puts each host endpoint back in audit mode within seconds of an agent restart, because any restart would otherwise start enforcing that node: a Renovate bump, a value change, Kured. Every node must answer `Enabled` before the policy merges:

   ```bash
   for p in $(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium -o name); do
     kubectl -n kube-system exec "$p" -c cilium-agent -- \
       sh -c 'cilium-dbg endpoint config $(cilium-dbg endpoint get -l reserved:host -o "jsonpath={\$[0].id}") | grep PolicyAuditMode'
   done
   ```
4. Merge the policy; it selects nothing. Select one worker, with its console within reach, and confirm `Disabled (Audit)` on its `reserved:host` line:

   ```bash
   kubectl label node <worker> host-firewall.wlkr.ch/selected=true
   kubectl -n kube-system exec <agent-on-worker> -c cilium-agent -- cilium-dbg endpoint list
   ```
5. Reboot that worker. It must return `Ready`, and audit mode `Enabled` within a minute; if it does not, go to [Host firewall lockout](<#host-firewall-lockout>) and stop the rollout.
6. Select the other workers, then one control plane and reboot it, then the other two. Only then start the audit week.
7. Read a week of what enforcement would refuse. Pods and nodes are admitted, so anything here came from the LAN. Add a rule for what is legitimate:

   ```text
   {job="hubble", verdict="AUDIT"} | json dst_id="flow.destination.identity", src="flow.IP.source", dst="flow.IP.destination", tcp="flow.l4.TCP.destination_port", udp="flow.l4.UDP.destination_port" | dst_id="1" | line_format "{{.src}} -> {{.dst}} {{.tcp}}{{.udp}}"
   ```
8. Enforce one worker: its label sends the DaemonSet away, and restarting its agent drops audit mode, rather than switching audit off at runtime. Check that `bpf policy get` lists separate identities and not one wildcard, and that SSH and the node's pods still work. Reboot it once more.

