   ```bash
   kubectl label node <worker> host-firewall.wlkr.ch/enforce=true
   kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l k8s-app=cilium --field-selector spec.nodeName=<worker>
   kubectl -n kube-system exec <agent-on-worker> -c cilium-agent -- cilium-dbg bpf policy get <host-endpoint-id>
   ```
9. Repeat for the workers, then the control planes one at a time. Then delete `payload/platform/cilium/host-firewall-audit.yaml` in a pull request.

## Health check

```bash
kubectl get ns -L pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce
kubectl get cnp -A
kubectl get ccnp
kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicy
```

## Pitfalls

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Audit mode stops at the proxy**
>
> `policyAuditMode` is a datapath setting. A request the Gateway's Envoy or an HTTP rule refuses is answered `403 Access denied` on the spot, and Hubble records it as a forwarded response, not an audited verdict. Look for it with `hubble observe --http-status 403`; in Loki the denied request is a `DROPPED` flow of type `REQUEST` whose source carries the caller's namespace and the `ingress` identity. The agents' `argocd` calls failed this way, `server: envoy` and `grpc-message: Access denied`, while their policy named the host but not the `argocd-server` pod; see [Agent account](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/#agent-account>).

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A name rule audits one SYN in twenty**
>
> A `toFQDNs` rule admits the addresses the DNS proxy has seen for the name, and the proxy releases the answer after at most 100ms whether or not every datapath has the new address. About one connection in twenty to a CDN name is recorded `AUDIT` with a `world` destination; under enforcement that `SYN` drops and the retransmit a second later goes through. A run of drops on one source port is different: the application connected to an address it cached past the DNS TTL.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The token change is not retroactive**
>
> The mount is decided at admission, so existing pods keep their token until recreated. That makes the change safe to roll out, and means a posture scan will not agree it is fixed until things restart.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **A reboot can isolate a node a host policy selects**
>
> [Upstream](<https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/48070>) reports a selected node on this same combination, tunnel, kube-proxy replacement and WireGuard, dropping everything after a cold boot or a runtime audit-off, until an out-of-band fix. It is open and unreproduced here, and a power cut would hit every selected node at once. That is why the rollout selects one worker first and reboots it.

## Recovery

### Host firewall lockout

Work down until the node answers. An agent that cannot reach the API server hears neither a policy change nor a label removal, so step 1 alone does not free a node that is already cut off.

1. API server answering: take the node out of the policy. Argo CD does not own node labels, so nothing puts it back. Use `--all` instead of a name for every node.

   ```bash
   kubectl label node <node> host-firewall.wlkr.ch/selected-
   ```
2. SSH answering: put the node in audit mode, which needs no API server and lasts until the agent restarts.

   ```bash
   ssh <node> sudo bash -s <<'EOF'
   id=$(crictl ps -q --label io.kubernetes.container.name=cilium-agent)
   crictl exec "$id" sh -c 'cilium-dbg endpoint config $(cilium-dbg endpoint get -l reserved:host -o "jsonpath={\$[0].id}") PolicyAuditMode=Enabled'
   EOF
   ```
3. Nothing answering, the API server up: nothing filters a node until its agent has started after boot, so stop the agent coming back. Run this from the workstation, then power-cycle the node, then do step 1 and start the kubelet again with `sudo systemctl unmask kubelet && sudo systemctl start kubelet`.

   ```bash
   until ssh -o ConnectTimeout=2 <node> sudo systemctl mask --now kubelet; do sleep 1; done
   ```
4. Every control plane cut off: the API server needs no CNI, so it comes up before the agent does. Power-cycle all three and take the label off in that window.

   ```bash
   until kubectl label node --all host-firewall.wlkr.ch/selected-; do sleep 2; done
   ```
5. Still nothing: at the node's console, add `flatcar.autologin` to the boot entry in the GRUB menu, since `core` has no password, then run the inner command of step 2. Failing that, [rebuild the node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/#rebuilding-or-repartitioning-a-node>).
6. Then [unseal OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/#after-any-node-reboot-unseal-openbao>) and revert in Git: the policy first; the switch only if the firewall itself is the fault, since that revert rolls every agent again.

# Tetragon

[Tetragon](<https://tetragon.io/>) watches processes at the kernel, with eBPF, on every node. Trivy says what an image *could* do; Tetragon records what a process *did*: every exec and exit in a pod, and, where a `TracingPolicy` says so, file opens and credential changes. It is the only thing here that sees a shell spawned in a running container.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system` |
| Depends on | Kernel BTF at `/sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux`, which Flatcar ships; [Logging](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) for the events, [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md>) for the alerts |
| If it is down | No runtime record and no runtime alerts; nothing else notices |
| Health check | `kubectl get tracingpolicies -o wide`; `TetragonPolicyNotLoaded` and `TetragonEventsLost` otherwise |
| Dashboard | [Tetragon](<https://monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch/d/tetragon-overview>): agent health, event rates, policy hits by binary, and the latest policy hits, shells and execs read from Loki |
| Files | `payload/platform/tetragon/`: the chart, the policies, `prometheusrule.yaml` and a dashboard written for this cluster, since upstream ships none |

## Configuration

Cilium's own chart, from `helm.cilium.io`; Tetragon does not depend on Cilium and runs privileged on the host network by the chart's default.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Export to stdout | The chart runs a sidecar that tails Tetragon's JSON file to stdout, so [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) collects it as any container log: `{namespace="kube-system", container="export-stdout"}` |
| `exportDenyList` | Exec and exit events from the host and from the platform's own `kube-system` pods, selected by label, stay out of the export; they are the bulk of the volume and the least interesting. Any other pod in `kube-system` is exported, because a stolen write role lands its privileged pod there. Policy hits still pass, which is the point of the `event_set` field |
| `enableProcessCred` | Capabilities and `privileges_changed` on every exec, so a setuid binary or a file-capability escalation is visible without a policy |
| Two `ServiceMonitor`s | `tetragon_policy_events_total` is what the alert reads; `tetragon_tracingpolicy_loaded` and the ring-buffer counters are its health |
| Memory limit | 2.5x the measured working set of the busiest agent with the policy library loaded, per the [platform rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/#components>); the dashboard's first row shows the current worst node against it |

### Policies

`tracingpolicies.yaml` carries the cluster-scoped `TracingPolicy` objects, adapted from the [upstream policy library](<https://tetragon.io/docs/policy-library/observability/>). All post at most one event per minute per selector, and most watch containers only, since the host has the node journal; `sensitive-file-access` and the signature hook of `kernel-module-load` record the host too. Every hook carries a `message` and one of upstream's `observability.*` tags, so an event says what it is without a lookup here.

| Policy | Hook | Fires on | Alerted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sensitive-file-access` | `security_file_permission` | A read of a control-plane or etcd key, the encryption config, an admin kubeconfig, etcd's data or a kubelet key, matched by the end of the path so a hostPath mounted anywhere counts, unless the reader is a control-plane binary, the kubelet, `kubeadm` or `kube-vip` on the host network, or the path is under `/run/cilium/state/`, where Cilium's route reconciler keeps its own `.wal`; the alert leaves out `etcdctl` in the etcd backup and defrag Jobs, by namespace and the `workload` label, which Tetragon sets to the CronJob's name, and `/proc/self/exe` in the `arc-jobs` workflow pods, which is buildah writing the account files of the image it builds; a read of `/etc/shadow` on the host by anything but PAM's `/sbin/unix_chkpwd`, which every login and `sudo` runs (in a container any read is PAM in the image, so only writes count there); any write, host or container, to `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/group`, `/etc/sudoers`, `/etc/ld.so.preload`, or under `/etc/sudoers.d/`, `/etc/cron.d/` and `/root/.ssh/` | Yes: `TetragonSensitiveFileAccess` |
| `process-creds-changed` | `commit_creds` | A container process that moved into another mount, pid, network or user namespace after its exec, except `runc`; the alert leaves out the `cilium` DaemonSet in `kube-system` and all of `rook-ceph`, whose init containers and OSD prepare Jobs `nsenter` into the host by design, and `/proc/self/exe` in the `arc-jobs` workflow pods, which is buildah re-executing itself into [its user namespace](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/index.md>). The hook runs on every execve and fork; the selector keeps the escape signal. Upstream's `matchCapabilityChanges` is not used: it matches a change in either direction, so every entrypoint that drops root fires it | Yes: `TetragonCredentialsEscalated` |
| `exec-from-writable-path` | `security_bprm_check` | A container executing a file under `/tmp/`, `/var/tmp/`, `/dev/shm/`, `/run/`, `/var/run/`, `/shared/`, `/controller/` or `/plugins/`, except the two binaries an init container copies there and the scripts s6-overlay writes under `/run/s6*` and `/run/service/` at start; the alert leaves out `go` in the `arc-jobs` workflow pods, which runs the test binaries it builds under `/tmp` | Yes: `TetragonExecFromWritablePath` |
| `library-from-writable-path` | `security_mmap_file` | The same paths mapped with `PROT_EXEC`, which is how a dropped shared library loads, except the native libraries runtimes unpack under `/tmp` on every start: Alloy's Snowflake driver (`/tmp/gosnowflake-cgo*`) and zstd-jni in Dependency-Track (`/tmp/libzstd-jni-*`); the alert leaves out `go` in the `arc-jobs` workflow pods | Yes: `TetragonLibraryFromWritablePath` |
| `privileges-raise`, `privileges-raise-gid`, `privileges-raise-gid-argocd` | The `__sys_set*uid` and `__sys_set*gid` family | Any setuid or setgid to root inside a container. A record: root re-asserting root is routine (`logrotate`), and a setuid binary that actually raises privileges is `TetragonPrivilegedExec`. `runc`, which sets the ids on every container start, is dropped in the kernel. The redis-ha busybox calls setgid on every applet, so the gid hooks leave out pods labelled `app: redis-ha` in `argocd` only; one `podSelector` cannot say "this label in that namespace", hence two gid policies | No |
| `bpf-program-load` | `bpf_check` | Any BPF program load from a container; the alert leaves out `cilium` and `kube-system` | Yes: `TetragonBpfProgramLoaded` |
| `kernel-module-load` | `security_kernel_module_request`, `security_kernel_read_file`, `find_module_sections` | A module requested by name or read from a container, minus the `net-pf-2-proto-262` and `net-pf-10-proto-262` requests Go binaries and haproxy make when they probe MPTCP at start and the `net-pf-31` one Home Assistant makes when it looks for a Bluetooth adapter; the alert leaves out `rook-ceph`, whose CSI plugin loads `rbd` after a boot. The third hook records every load's signature check, host included: Flatcar signs its modules but does not enforce it (`CONFIG_MODULE_SIG` without `_FORCE`) | Yes: `TetragonKernelModuleLoaded`; `TetragonUnsignedKernelModule` from Loki |
| `dns-outside-cluster` | `ip_output` | A port 53 packet from a container to anything but the kube-dns ClusterIP or the pod range, which is a hard-coded resolver in an image, a tunnel or exfiltration. The pod range is left out because it holds each node's Cilium router address, the pod's default gateway, which Home Assistant's dhcp integration asks for PTR records at start. The hook sees TCP and UDP alike, so musl's unconnected sends count too; the alert leaves out `kube-system`, where CoreDNS forwards upstream, and `cert-manager`, whose DNS-01 propagation check asks the zone's authoritative servers | Yes: `TetragonDnsOutsideCluster` |
| `mount-in-container` | `security_sb_mount` | Any mount from a container except by `runc`, which mounts the rootfs, proc and sysfs on every start. Escapes start with a mount of the host's disk, cgroup or proc; the alert leaves out `rook-ceph`, `cilium` and `kube-system`, which mount by design, and `/proc/self/exe` in the `arc-jobs` workflow pods, which is buildah mounting in its user namespace | Yes: `TetragonMountInContainer` |
| `ptrace-in-container` | `security_ptrace_access_check` | An attach-mode access to another process from a container: ptrace, `process_vm_writev`, `/proc/<pid>/mem`. The read mode `ps` uses is left alone | Yes: `TetragonPtraceInContainer` |
| `kill-unprivileged-user-namespace` | `create_user_ns` | A user namespace created without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in a container, killed, except in `arc-jobs`. The only policy in `enforce` mode | Yes: `TetragonUserNamespaceCreated` |
| `unprivileged-user-namespace-arc-jobs` | `create_user_ns` | The same in `arc-jobs`, recorded: buildah builds the images there in a user namespace, see [GitHub runners](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/index.md>) | No; every image build would fire it |
| `egress-outside-cluster` | `security_socket_connect` | An IPv4 `connect()`, TCP or UDP, from a container to anything outside the pod, service and site ranges | No; ACME, S3, the Trivy database and Home Assistant all do this routinely |

The allow list in the first policy is the set of things that read key material in steady state, found by listing what fired. Add a binary there only after confirming it in the export; a person running `cat` on a node is exactly what the policy is for. A binary path is only trusted together with the host network namespace: any image can ship `/usr/local/bin/etcd`, but only a privileged namespace can run it with `hostNetwork`. The exemption stays in the kernel rather than on pod labels, because the `podSelector` pitfall below would miss a pod that reads a key the moment it starts; exemptions by namespace and workload go in the alert instead.

The third policy is the runtime half of an image check: nothing in an image lives on those paths, so a binary executing from one was written after the container started. An emptyDir can be mounted anywhere, so the policy names the mounts this cluster puts binaries into rather than every emptyDir; `kubectl get pods -A -o json` lists the rest. A `readOnlyRootFilesystem` pod makes the check complete, since then a new binary has nowhere else to land. The offline half, every binary Tetragon saw executed diffed against the image's file list, needs no policy: query Loki by image and binary and resolve each path in `crane export <image> - | tar t`.

Four more detections from the same library need no policy, because the exec event already carries what they look for: `sudo`, a setuid or file-capability binary raising privileges, a fileless exec and a deleted binary. They are [Loki alerts](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/#alerting>). Upstream's `sshd` policy is covered by `NodeSshLogin` from the node journal.

## Usage

The dashboard is the summary; the queries below are what its Loki panels run.

```text
# Everything a policy caught
{namespace="kube-system", container="export-stdout"} | json | process_kprobe_policy_name!=""

# Every exec in one namespace, with arguments
{namespace="kube-system", container="export-stdout"} | json | process_exec_process_pod_namespace="home-assistant"
  | line_format "{{.process_exec_process_binary}} {{.process_exec_process_arguments}}"
```

The `tetra` CLI in the agent pod does the same live:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- tetra getevents -o compact --namespaces home-assistant
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get ds tetragon
kubectl get tracingpolicies -o wide     # STATE should be enabled
```

### Enforcement

Every policy but one only records. `kill-unprivileged-user-namespace` carries `policy-mode: enforce` and a `Sigkill`, because nothing here creates user namespaces and most kernel escalation chains start with one. It stays scoped to containers: a sysctl would cover the host too, where systemd's `PrivateUsers=` needs them. The one exception is `arc-jobs`, where buildah needs one for every image build; its `podSelector` excludes that namespace, at the price of the first seconds of every container (see Pitfalls), and a monitor-only twin records the events there. The limits, both checked on the running nodes: `Override` and enforcers need `CONFIG_FUNCTION_ERROR_INJECTION`, which Flatcar's kernel does not set, and BPF LSM hooks need `bpf` in the `lsm=` boot argument, which Flatcar does not pass. That leaves `Sigkill`, which upstream warns does not stop an operation already in flight. A policy without `policy-mode` loads in monitor mode and its kill actions are elided, so an enforcing policy has to say so.

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A `podSelector` misses a pod's first seconds**
>
> The policy filter learns pods from the API and maps their cgroups; a process that runs the moment a container starts is not yet selected, and the test pod's `unshare` went unrecorded by the filtered policy while the unfiltered one killed it. Put the hook an alert depends on in a policy without a `podSelector`, and do exclusions in PromQL.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A first hit is a new series, and `increase()` of one sample is zero**
>
> `tetragon_policy_events_total` has a pod label, so the first hit from a pod creates a counter series inside the alert window and `increase()` reports nothing until the second scrape moves it. Every policy alert therefore also matches a series absent one window earlier, with `unless ... offset`, and holds with `keep_firing_for`, because the agent drops a pod's series when the pod exits and a one-shot pod would otherwise flap. Copy that shape for a new alert, and test it with a pod that fires once, not with one that keeps firing.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **An exclusion has to outlive the pod**
>
> `increase(...[10m])` still sees a pod's events for ten minutes after the agent dropped its series, while a bare selector on the right of `unless` matches nothing once the series is stale, so a left-out one-shot pod fires when it exits. Write every exclusion as `unless on (...) last_over_time(...[10m])`, the same window as the `increase()`.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A policy that does not load is silent**
>
> A `TracingPolicy` naming a kernel function this kernel does not export sits in state `error` and watches nothing. `TetragonPolicyNotLoaded` fires after its `for`; check `kubectl get tracingpolicies -o wide` after every Flatcar release that moves the kernel.

# Trivy Operator

Aqua Security's [Trivy Operator](<https://aquasecurity.github.io/trivy-operator/latest/>) scans everything the cluster runs and writes every result back as a Kubernetes object. Reading those objects is [Vulnerability Triage](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/vulnerabilities/index.md>); this page is the operator itself.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `trivy-system` |
| Depends on | [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md>) for the `ServiceMonitor` and the dashboard, [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for the vulnerability database volume |
| If it is down | Reports expire after `scannerReportTTL` and are not rebuilt; `TrivyContainerNotScanned` fires for every container |
| Health check | `kubectl -n trivy-system get pods,jobs`, then the reconciliation below |
| Dashboard | [Trivy Operator](<https://monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch/d/trivy-operator-overview>) |
| Files | `payload/platform/trivy-operator/`: the chart, `prometheusrule.yaml`, the `findings-history` and `report-prune` CronJobs, the `sbom-readers.yaml` grant and a dashboard written for this cluster. The namespace labels and the default-deny policy are in [Security Policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md>) |

| Scanner | Produces | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vulnerability | `VulnerabilityReport` | Which CVEs are in the images we run |
| Exposed secret | `ExposedSecretReport` | Which images have credentials baked in |
| Config audit | `ConfigAuditReport` | Which workloads are misconfigured |
| RBAC assessment | `RbacAssessmentReport` | Which roles grant too much |
| Infra assessment | `InfraAssessmentReport` | Whether the nodes pass CIS |
| Compliance | `ClusterComplianceReport` | CIS 1.23, NSA/CISA 1.0, PSS baseline and restricted |

The `eks-` and `rke2-` compliance specs are for other distributions and are left out rather than reported as failing.

## Configuration

The values in `application.yaml` that are not defaults:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `scannerReportTTL`, `vulnerabilityScannerScanOnlyCurrentRevisions`, `configAuditScannerScanOnlyCurrentRevisions`, `scanJobTTL` | Reports live in etcd. A stale report is rebuilt, superseded ReplicaSets are not scanned, and finished jobs do not accumulate |
| `builtInTrivyServer: true` | `ClientServer` mode: one `trivy-server` holds the vulnerability database on the PVC. Standalone mode downloads it in every scan job, which meets registry rate limits, and a rate-limited scan reports zero findings rather than an error |
| `ignoreUnfixed: false`, every severity | A finding with no fix is usually the signal that the base image is wrong, and a finding the scanner could not grade is worth reading |
| `ignorePolicy.authentik` | The image carries thousands of unfixed Debian findings and its reports exceed the etcd request limit. The Rego (v0 syntax, `object.get` because `FixedVersion` is absent when there is no fix) drops only findings that have no fix *and* are below HIGH |
| `skipFiles` | Debian's placeholder key in every CloudNativePG image, which serves TLS from certificates of its own, would otherwise sit in every Postgres report. Trivy's Rego input for a secret has no path, so an ignore policy could only drop the `private-key` rule and every real key with it; this skips one exact path |
| `additionalVulnerabilityReportFields` without `Description` and `Links` | A report is one API write, capped at 2 MiB; `Links` alone is over half the payload. An oversized report is rejected with nothing but an operator log line |
| `operator.scanJobTimeout` and `trivy.timeout`, kept equal | The first is the Job's `activeDeadlineSeconds` and kills the pod whatever Trivy is doing; the second is Trivy's own flag and only fires if it is the shorter. Raising one alone does nothing |
| `accessGlobalSecretsAndServiceAccount: false` | The default grants the operator read on every Secret in the cluster so scan jobs can borrow a workload's `imagePullSecrets`, and every image here is public. A private image would fail its scan and raise `TrivyContainerNotScanned`. The flag also drops `nodes/proxy`, without which node-collector silently skips the kubelet-configuration CIS checks, so `node-collector-rbac.yaml` grants that back |
| `clusterSbomCacheEnabled: false` | With the cache, every workload after the first to use an image gets an `SbomReport` from the cached SBOM and no `VulnerabilityReport`. Upstream: [trivy-operator\#1668](<https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy-operator/issues/1668>) |
| `configFile` with `scan.skip-version-check` and `scan.disable-telemetry` | The operator mounts it into every scan job as `trivy.yaml`. Trivy's version check and its usage telemetry share one request to `check.trivy.dev`, so switching off one still sends it; the server never makes the call, only the scan jobs |
| `metricsVulnIdEnabled: false` | One series per CVE per container is a six-figure cardinality, and every label is already in the report |
| `compliance.reportType: summary` | The collector skips reports in `all` format, so `trivy_compliance_info` disappears and the dashboard's failing-controls table empties. The `status` label is title-cased: `Fail`, `Pass` |
| Control-plane tolerations on `nodeCollector` and `scanJobTolerations` | Without them the CIS infra assessment covers only the workers and reports a clean control plane it never looked at |
| `enforce: privileged`, `audit`/`warn: restricted` on the namespace, in `payload/platform/security/pod-security.yaml` | node-collector hostPath-mounts `/var/lib/etcd`, `/var/lib/kubelet`, `/etc/kubernetes` and `/etc/cni/net.d`, which `baseline` forbids. Scan jobs themselves drop all capabilities and run read-only |
| `resources` on the operator | Its cache holds every report in the cluster, and the `SbomReport`s are most of that. At the limit it is OOM-killed mid-write, which shows as reports that never appear rather than as an error |
| `logDevMode: false` | Its `V(1)` lines are the only way to see decisions the operator makes silently, but it switches logging to console encoding. Turn it on to debug, then off |

### Alerting

The rules in `prometheusrule.yaml`. Reports expire and are rebuilt every `scannerReportTTL`, so a "new" finding is one absent from the reports two days ago rather than from the previous scrape, and every rule waits longer than a rebuild.

| Alert | Fires when | Why this shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TrivyContainerNotScanned` | A running container has had no `VulnerabilityReport` for 2h | A rejected report is never written, so it looks identical to a clean one; only reconciling against what runs finds it |
| `TrivyExposedSecretNew` | A secret finding, by rule and path, was in no report two days ago, whichever container carried it | An accepted finding never clears, so an absolute rule would fire forever; and the same finding in a new pod is not new |
| `TrivyRbacCriticalNew` | A Role or ClusterRole gains a critical finding it did not have two days ago | Every critical ClusterRole is a chart's operator role or Kubernetes' own, see [Vulnerability Triage](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/vulnerabilities/#what-is-load-bearing>); what matters is a new one |
| `TrivyConfigAuditCritical` | Any workload fails a critical config-audit check for 2h | Nothing does today, so the rule is absolute |
| `TrivyComplianceRegression` | A framework has more failing controls than a day ago, for 12h | Compliance is recomputed every six hours; two runs above yesterday is drift, not a rebuild |

The two "new" rules also require the operator to have been reporting two days ago, so a fresh cluster does not page on every existing finding.

`TrivyContainerNotScanned` compares every running container against the containers that have a `VulnerabilityReport` and names the difference:

```promql
count by (namespace, container) (
  kube_pod_container_info
  * on (namespace, pod) group_left ()
  (max by (namespace, pod) (kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Running"} == 1))
)
unless on (namespace, container)
count by (namespace, container) (
  label_replace(trivy_image_info, "container", "$1", "container_name", "(.+)")
)
```

- **Keyed on `(namespace, container)`, not the digest**: containerd's platform digest and the registry's tag digest differ permanently for mirrored images.
- **Restricted to `Running` pods**, or every completed Job counts as unscanned.
- **A `for` of several full sweeps**, so the TTL churn does not page.

The dashboard's stat and by-severity panels take `max by (image_digest)` before summing, and workload panels join ReplicaSets against `kube_replicaset_spec_replicas > 0`, so a finding counts once per image and a superseded revision drops out. The "Worst workloads" table stays per container on purpose: it answers where a finding runs.

### History

Reports live for `scannerReportTTL` and Prometheus for its `retention`, so neither can answer whether a count went up over a quarter. The `findings-history` CronJob in `findings-history.yaml` lists every report kind once a day and prints one JSON line per namespace, and per compliance framework, to stdout; Alloy ships it like any container log and Loki keeps that one stream far longer than the rest (`retention_stream` in `loki/application.yaml`). The dashboard's last row reads it. Images are counted once per digest per namespace, the same rule the dashboard applies.

```text
{namespace="trivy-system", container="findings-history"} | json | kind="vulnerabilities" | namespace="argocd"
```

### SBOM export

`sbomGenerationEnabled` makes the operator write one CycloneDX `SbomReport` per container next to the `VulnerabilityReport`. Nothing here reads them; [Dependency-Track](<https://homelab-apps.wlkr.ch/dependency-track/>) in the workloads repository uploads every one of them nightly and keeps the history Trivy's 24h reports cannot. `sbom-readers.yaml` is the `ClusterRole` and binding that let its upload job list them, and the ReplicaSets, so it can skip the reports of superseded revisions: the `apps` project may not create cluster-scoped RBAC, and which workload reads the operator's findings is decided here.

### Report pruning

`SbomReport`s and `ExposedSecretReport`s carry no TTL, unlike the `VulnerabilityReport`s: they are owned by the scanned ReplicaSet and live as long as it does, and Deployments keep ten superseded revisions scaled to zero. Those SBOMs were over half the reports' bytes in etcd, and each API server holds them decoded in its watch cache. The `report-prune` CronJob in `report-prune.yaml` deletes the two kinds for every ReplicaSet scaled to zero, daily before the Dependency-Track upload, which skips those reports anyway. The two `ScanOnlyCurrentRevisions` settings keep the operator from writing them again. Its log is one JSON line per kind with the count deleted.

## Usage

The dashboard is a summary; the objects have the detail.

```bash
# What has been scanned, worst first
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -A --sort-by='.report.summary.criticalCount'

# The findings themselves, for one workload
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -n <ns> <name> -o json \
  | jq '.report.vulnerabilities[]
        | select(.severity=="CRITICAL")
        | {id: .vulnerabilityID, pkg: .resource,
           installed: .installedVersion, fixed: .fixedVersion}'

# Misconfiguration, RBAC and node checks
kubectl get configauditreports -A
kubectl get rbacassessmentreports,clusterrbacassessmentreports -A
kubectl get infraassessmentreports -A

# Which compliance controls are failing
kubectl get clustercompliancereports k8s-cis-1.23 -o json \
  | jq '.status.summary, (.status.summaryReport.controlCheck[]
        | select(.totalFail > 0))'
```

## Health check

Reconcile running containers against scanned ones, keyed on `(namespace, container)` like the alert; the output is every running container with no `VulnerabilityReport`, and healthy is an empty output:

```bash
comm -23 \
  <(kubectl get pods -A --field-selector status.phase=Running -o json \
      | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace as $ns | .spec.containers[] | "\($ns) \(.name)"' | sort -u) \
  <(kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -A -o json \
      | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.metadata.namespace) \(.metadata.labels["trivy-operator.container.name"])"' | sort -u)
```

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Zero is not the same as clean**
>
> A report that reads zero may be a clean image or a scan that failed: a rate-limited pull, a timeout, an image the operator could not resolve. Check the object exists and carries a real digest before believing a zero, and look at `kubectl -n trivy-system get jobs` when one never appears. This is where the `vulnerability-triage` skill in `.claude/skills/` starts.

## Pitfalls

Four ways a workload ends up with no `VulnerabilityReport`, all silent from the outside:

| Symptom | Cause | Where to look |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No report, no `SbomReport`, operator logs `ResourceExhausted ... larger than max` or `etcdserver: request is too large` | The report exceeds the API write ceiling | Operator log. Fix: the fields and ignore policies above |
| No report, Job events show `DeadlineExceeded` | `scanJobTimeout` elapsed on a large image | `kubectl -n trivy-system get events --field-selector reason=DeadlineExceeded`, before `scanJobTTL` deletes the Job |
| Some containers of a multi-container workload missing; job succeeded; log has `failed to analyze layer ... unexpected EOF` | A scan container died reading the image and the operator keeps only containers that exited 0. Hits workloads with several containers on one image (Rook, Cilium). Not the shared cache: concurrent scans with it pass | Scan job pod logs |
| Reports missing at random, operator restart count climbing, last state `OOMKilled` | The report cache outgrew the memory limit | `kubectl -n trivy-system get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=trivy-operator -o jsonpath='{..lastState}'`. Fix: `resources` in `application.yaml` |
| `SbomReport` exists, no `VulnerabilityReport` | SBOM cache reuse path ran `trivy sbom` and produced nothing | Confirm `clusterSbomCacheEnabled` is off |

A completed scan job counts against `concurrentScanJobsLimit` until `scanJobTTL` deletes it, so a backlog drains in batches of the limit, the chart's default, once per TTL; that is the expected shape, not a stall.

# Velero

[Velero](<https://velero.io/>) backs up Kubernetes objects and, through CSI snapshots and its data mover, the data in every PVC, nightly into a bucket in the Ceph object store. What it covers, what it does not, and the restore runbooks are in [Backups &amp; Recovery](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md>); this page is the chart tuning.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `backup` |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for the bucket claims and RBD snapshots |
| If it is down | Nightly backups stop; `VeleroBackupTooOld` fires once the last success is older than the rule's threshold |
| Health check | `kubectl -n backup get backupstoragelocation` reads `Available` |
| Files | `payload/platform/velero/`, `payload/platform/backup/`, `payload/platform/snapshot-controller/` |

## Configuration

In `application.yaml`'s `valuesObject` unless a file is named:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `checksumAlgorithm: ""` on the `BackupStorageLocation` | The AWS plugin's SDK sends a trailing checksum that Ceph RGW rejects with `XAmzContentSHA256Mismatch`; every upload fails without it |
| `s3Url: https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch`, not the RGW Service | kopia's S3 client signs plain-HTTP uploads with the streaming SigV4 scheme, which Ceph RGW rejects as unsigned headers since [CVE-2026-54330](<https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/security/CVE-2026-54330/>); over TLS it sends `UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD` and RGW accepts it. The infra Gateway terminates TLS with the Let's Encrypt wildcard, so no CA has to reach Velero or the movers |
| `velero-plugin-for-aws` init container | The plugin minor must match the chart's Velero appVersion; the chart's commented example is one line behind |
| `credentials.useSecret: false` with `extraEnvVars` | Keys come from the environment, fed by the `Secret` Rook writes for the `velero-bucket` claim; nothing is rendered into a file or Git |
| `defaultSnapshotMoveData`, `deployNodeAgent`, `uploaderType: kopia` | A CSI snapshot is a Ceph object in the same cluster; the data mover (run by the node agent) streams it into the bucket and deletes the snapshot |
| `volumeSnapshotLocation: []` | The chart's placeholder renders a `VolumeSnapshotLocation` the CRD rejects, failing every sync; Helm replaces lists, so the empty list removes it |
| `VolumeSnapshotClass` in `payload/platform/backup/volumesnapshotclass.yaml` | The `velero.io/csi-volumesnapshot-class` label is how Velero finds the class; without it volumes are skipped silently. `deletionPolicy: Delete`, because the durable copy is the data mover's |
| `snapshot-controller` Application | Neither kubeadm nor Rook installs the CSI snapshot controller or its CRDs, which must exist before the `VolumeSnapshotClass` applies, so it is its own Application. It applies the two kustomize directories [kubernetes-csi/external-snapshotter](<https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-snapshotter>) publishes at each tag, the owning project's only packaging, namespaced into `backup` with the hardening as a patch and the image pinned to the tag, because the Deployment upstream publishes at a tag still names the previous release's image, so Renovate moves the two together — see [Maintenance](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/maintenance/#automerge-policy>); upstream ships no PDB for its two leader-elected replicas, so `pdb.yaml` adds one |
| No `runAsNonRoot` on the `velero` container | Whether the plugin init container's copy into `/target` works non-root depends on the image's `USER`; confirm on a real backup first |
| Node agent `containerSecurityContext` | Root and capabilities stay because kopia reads every pod volume; escalation is off and seccomp is on |
| `prometheusRule` | Four rules: `VeleroBackupFailures` (critical) and `VeleroBackupPartialFailures` (warning) on a schedule's outcome, `VeleroBackupTooOld` (critical), the only one that catches a backup hanging `InProgress`, and `VeleroBackupInProgress` (info), which is [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/#configuration>)'s reboot gate rather than a problem to mail |

### Repository password

Kopia encrypts the volume data in every repository with one password, read from the Secret `velero-repo-credentials` (key `repository-password`) in Velero's namespace. When that Secret is missing Velero creates it with a default compiled into the binary, which protects nothing, so `payload/platform/backup/velero-repo-credentials.yaml` supplies it.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| A `Password` generator and `PushSecret` writing `velero/repository` | A [generated secret](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/#generated-secrets>): random, written once, and in the OpenBao snapshot that a restore on a fresh cluster needs anyway |
| `creationPolicy: Owner` on the `ExternalSecret` | ESO takes over the Secret Velero created at start-up and overwrites the default |
| `velero.io/exclude-from-backup` on the Secret | The resource backup lands in the same bucket as the repositories the password unlocks |
| Secrets stay in the resource backup | The tarball under `backups/` is not encrypted, so every backed-up `Secret` sits in the bucket as JSON. Excluding them would break a namespace restore: CloudNativePG, the bucket claims, cert-manager and Argo CD generate Secrets that exist nowhere else. The `velero` bucket and its keys are therefore as sensitive as an unencrypted etcd |

A repository keeps the password it was initialised with, and all repositories share one, so a changed value makes every existing repository unreachable; see [Re-initialising the repositories](<#re-initialising-the-repositories>).

## Usage

```bash
velero -n backup backup create manual-$(date +%s) --include-namespaces my-app
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n backup get backupstoragelocation       # Available
kubectl -n backup get backups.velero.io           # Completed, not PartiallyFailed
kubectl -n backup get volumesnapshotclass rook-ceph-block
kubectl -n backup get backuprepositories.velero.io  # Ready
kubectl -n backup get externalsecret velero-repo-credentials   # SecretSynced
```

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **PartiallyFailed with no volume data**
>
> Velero found no labelled `VolumeSnapshotClass` and skipped every volume without an error. Check the class above exists and carries the label.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Every `BackupRepository` NotReady, `Access Denied` on `kopia.blobcfg`**
>
> Objects upload, volume data does not: the RGW log shows `PUT /velero/kopia/...` from `minio-go` with no authenticated user while the AWS SDK's PUTs succeed. The S3 URL is plain HTTP again; see the `s3Url` row above.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Every `BackupRepository` NotReady, `invalid repository password`**
>
> The password changed under existing repositories: OpenBao was rebuilt without its snapshot, `velero/repository` was deleted, or a backup ran on a fresh cluster before OpenBao was unsealed and initialised them with Velero's default. Volume data stops and backups end `PartiallyFailed`. Restore the old value into OpenBao if it exists anywhere; otherwise re-initialise as below.

## Recovery

### Re-initialising the repositories

Discards every backup in the bucket, resource backups included: a `Backup` whose volume snapshots cannot be reached never finishes deleting, so the bucket is emptied as a whole and Velero drops the `Backup` objects it no longer finds there.

1. Confirm the Secret carries the value from OpenBao, not Velero's default.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n backup get externalsecret velero-repo-credentials   # SecretSynced
   ```
2. Delete the repository objects.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n backup delete backuprepositories.velero.io --all
   ```
3. Empty the bucket with its own keys, from a machine that reaches the infra Gateway.

   ```bash
   export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(kubectl -n backup get secret velero-bucket -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}' | base64 -d)
   export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(kubectl -n backup get secret velero-bucket -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}' | base64 -d)
   export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=$(mktemp)    # path-style addressing, without touching ~/.aws
   printf '[default]\ns3 =\n    addressing_style = path\n' > "$AWS_CONFIG_FILE"
   aws --endpoint-url https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch --region eu-central-1 s3 rm s3://velero --recursive
   ```
4. Restart Velero and the node agents, so no cached repository connection survives.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n backup rollout restart deployment/velero daemonset/node-agent
   ```
5. Take a backup now rather than at the next schedule, and confirm it.

   ```bash
   velero -n backup backup create --from-schedule velero-daily
   kubectl -n backup get backups.velero.io               # Completed
   kubectl -n backup get backuprepositories.velero.io    # Ready
   ```
